 Fi Wi Land: From their first steps, Jamaica’s sea turtles must be protected 







Once abundant along the island’s shores and in its surrounding waters, Jamaica’s sea turtles now face mounting threats to their survival. From habitat loss caused by coastal development, tourism and beach erosion to poaching and natural predators, these marine creatures face numerous challenges, particularly during the vulnerable nesting and hatching seasons.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, host Carlysia Ramdeen and National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) Environmental Coordinator Ricardo Miller explore the importance of protecting Jamaica’s sea turtles and the role everyone can play in their conservation.

They discuss what to do when encountering nesting turtles or newly hatched babies, why disturbing nesting sites can have serious consequences, and how simple, responsible actions can give hatchlings a better chance of survival.

Discover how you can help safeguard these threatened marine creatures for future generations as the Jamaica Observer, in association with NEPA, presents Episode 2 of Fi Wi Land.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

 Bad Sekki to make first US trip in November after securing visa 







Popular Jamaican comedian and content creator Karlando “Bad Sekki” Bailey is set to travel to the United States for the first time on November 16 after securing a US visa earlier this month.

Bailey, who was previously denied a visa in March 2025, successfully reapplied this year and is now preparing for a 17-day trip across four American cities under the project Bad Sekki Goes to America, which will run from November 16 to December 2.

“I felt happy and really thankful that I got it. I tried last year and didn’t get it,” Bailey said.

According to Jason McNeish, CEO of Creative Factory which houses The Influence JA, travelling to the United States has long been a dream for the comedian, who was eager to depart almost immediately after receiving the good news.

“He wanted to go the next day after he got the passport but we wanted to make it a whole trip. He will be visiting four cities so it took a longer time to plan,” McNeish explained.

The visit will see Bailey reconnecting with relatives, creating content and exploring opportunities for professional development, including visits to production studios.

McNeish also revealed that discussions are underway to facilitate a possible engagement with Netflix, although arrangements have not yet been confirmed.

“We are making it a full experience, he’s going to of course connect with family and more importantly for me he is going to get some professional development as well, so we are looking at visiting a few

studios overseas and we are looking at Netflix,” he said.

For Bailey, one of the highlights of the upcoming trip will be visiting New York City’s famous Times Square, where he hopes to film a video he has envisioned for years.

“A just one video idea me have weh me really wah do from when, where I am in Time Square saying ‘New York’. That’s the main thing I am looking forward to,” he shared while laughing.

The comedian, who rose to prominence through humorous videos inspired by his experiences as a security guard, has become one of Jamaica’s popular social media personalities.

His upcoming trip will be documented through Bad Sekki Goes to America, giving followers a front-row seat to his first visit to the United States.

news.title: EU gas prices hit four-year high amid Iran war
news.text:
European natural gas prices have surged to their highest level in four years amid the war in Iran and the EU’s continued push to phase out Russian energy supplies, according to data from online aggregator Trading Economics.

On Monday, wholesale prices briefly surpassed €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour, reaching levels not seen since December 2022. The increase came as the bloc’s gas storage facilities were just 74.62% full as of October 25, well below seasonal averages.

Liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for around a fifth of global LNG trade before the US and Israeli military campaign against Iran earlier this year, remained approximately 80% below pre-conflict levels.

Some EU countries have already begun drawing on stored gas as temperatures fall. Trading Economics forecasts that European gas prices will reach €98.20 per megawatt-hour by the end of the fourth quarter of 2026.

In the UK, the month-ahead gas contract rose by 4% to its highest level since December 2022, according to the Guardian. Brent crude, which climbed to $117 per barrel last week, has since eased slightly but remains around $115.

British households could face a 27% increase in energy bills in January, pushing the average annual dual-fuel bill to nearly £2,200 ($2,940), according to a forecast by energy supplier EDF. An earlier forecast by consultancy Cornwall Insight had projected a 16% increase to approximately £2,000.

In August, the Guardian reported mounting concerns in the EU over low gas storage levels and soaring prices ahead of winter. In September, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen warned that the bloc was facing its worst energy crisis since 2022.

In mid-October, German media reported that Berlin was planning to make households and businesses pay for a national emergency gas reserve costing more than €3 billion over ten years. The government-controlled stockpile would be reserved for emergencies, including sabotage and infrastructure failures, rather than used to lower gas prices.

The reports came as the opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) party called for restoring energy ties with Russia and following US President Donald Trump’s example. On October 13, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said Germany should seek its own diesel deal with Moscow, praising Trump’s agreement with Russia as a pragmatic approach.

Following the EU’s sweeping sanctions on Russia in 2022, the bloc experienced one of its worst energy crises in decades. Gas prices soared above €300 per megawatt-hour, driving up costs for industries and households and contributing to surging inflation.

The EU has continued its efforts to phase out Russian energy. While Russia accounted for around 45% of the bloc’s gas imports in 2021, its share had fallen to approximately 12% by 2025.

Moscow has described the EU’s efforts to sever energy ties with Russia as a “suicidal” policy. Last week, Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued that the bloc would eventually have to restore those ties because “cooperation with Russia economically will be inevitable.”

Dmitriev also blamed the EU’s current problems, including high energy costs, on the bloc’s leaders, accusing them of refusing to acknowledge and correct their mistakes.
news.summary:
European gas prices have hit a four-year high as the Iran war disrupts LNG shipments and low storage levels fuel concerns ahead of winter

 Football legend Ronaldinho to play in Jamaica 







Brazilian football legend Ronaldinho will touch down in Jamaica for a series of events from December 3-7, his visit coinciding with the honoring of the 1998 Reggae Boyz World Cup squad.

news.title: Trump offers $1 million for tipoffs that lead to voter fraud convictions
news.text:
President Donald Trump said on Monday that the US would give $1 million to anyone who reported voter fraud that leads to an arrest and conviction, a week before midterm elections that polls show could prove difficult for his Republican Party.

The Trump administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, for example by pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.

“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

Some election officials have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in midterm elections. Trump has made false claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 elections. His supporters eventually stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, in an unsuccessful attempt to prevent congressional certification of those elections.

Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the House of Representatives and Senate. However, ahead of the midterm vote in which control of Congress is at stake, Trump’s approval has remained low due to voter concerns about the high cost of living and rising fuel prices from the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Published on October 27, 2026
news.summary: Offer comes a week before midterms as Republicans face difficult polls and low approval over living costs and Iran war fuel prices

news.title: Trump's bid to block California mail ballots over 'non-citizens' hits court roadblock
news.text: A US appeals court on Monday rejected the US President Donald Trump administration’s request to stop California from counting mail ballots cast by people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters whom the federal government suspects may be “non-citizens”.The 2-1 ruling by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked a setback for Trump’s efforts to expand the federal government’s role in overseeing elections ahead of the November 3 midterm polls. Reuters reported.Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress.The appeals court majority said the Justice Department had not given a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, making it premature for the appeals court to intervene. The lower court has scheduled a hearing for Tuesday.Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, said in a concurring opinion that the federal government was asking the court to direct a state legislature on an issue traditionally under state control. He warned that doing so could disrupt existing policies and create confusion for voters and election officials.Mail ballots are paper ballots sent to a voter's home address, allowing them to vote remotely rather than going to a polling place in person.The lawsuit marks an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting. It was the first time the administration had sought to prevent a state from counting votes, although it has not said how many people on the list had actually submitted mail ballots.Justice Department officials said on October 19 that 28 of the more than 20,000 people had been criminally charged with illegally voting. Reuters reported.California, the most populous US state, is a democratic stronghold and has 52 seats in the House of Representatives, more than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the chamber from Republicans in the midterm elections.Trump has made California a focus of his immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing the state’s sanctuary policies, which limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, of undermining public safety. He has also alleged that the state’s immigration policies have enabled voter fraud.The Justice Department has warned election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allow noncitizens to remain on voter rolls or cast ballots. It has also sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls containing sensitive personal information, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning any, as per Reuters.Voting rights activists have warned that the administration’s methods of checking voter lists could wrongly identify naturalised US citizens as noncitizens and lead to their removal from voter rolls.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: A US appeals court denied the Trump administration's request to prevent California from counting mail ballots from alleged 'non-citizens'. This ruling is part of the administration's ongoing efforts regarding voter eligibility and non-citizen voting. The Justice Department claimed some individuals on the voter list were charged with illegal voting. Voting rights activists expressed concern over potential misidentification of naturalised citizens as non-citizens.

news.title: Heckler slams Donald Trump during rally speech over White House ballroom as President yells 'oh, go home'
news.text: A heckler at President Donald Trump 's midterm rally was escorted out by security after shouting about the White House ballroom and interrupting Trump's speech on Monday evening. The protester began shouting about the White House ballroom before being escorted away by two security guards, the Mirror US reports , shown in live footage from the rally in Mississippi. The ballroom is among several renovation projects that the real estate mogul and former reality TV star has embarked on during his second term, sparking major backlash across the political spectrum for overhauling the historic landmark of the White House. Trump, 80, immediately branded the heckler a "paid protestor" given $250 by billionaire George Soros to disrupt the event, without any evidence. The president then told the heckler repeatedly, "oh, go home", as he faced the disruption during his speech in the southern state. "They think it's Soros. And they ruin their lives. They get booked. We don't usually press it that hard. It's terrible," Trump continued. Live footage from the rally shows two security officers walking the man, dressed in a red hoodie, out of the venue as the animated crowd "boo'd" and chanted "USA! USA! USA!" while throwing thumbs down in his face as he left the rally. "I was just at the punchline, too!" Trump added, after an attendee could be heard shouting, "We love you!" The Trump-led $400 million ballroom project required the demolition of the century-old East Wing of the White House in October 2025, a move that enraged some Americans. "President Trump is a builder at heart and has an extraordinary eye for detail. "The President and the Trump White House are fully committed to working with the appropriate organisations to preserving the special history of the White House while building a beautiful ballroom that can be enjoyed by future Administrations and generations of Americans to come," said White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The incident occurred at one of the many rallies Trump has attended to boost Republican candidates in the final crunch before the midterm election on Tuesday, November 3. Some of the rallies have been in historically red states that are in danger of flipping in what is expected to be a bloodbath for Republicans. Trump was stumping for incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) ahead of his race with Democratic nominee Scott Colom, an African-American district attorney, for the historically Republican Senate seat. Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.
news.summary: The United States President immediately branded the heckler a 'paid protester', before crowds booed and chanted 'USA! USA!', and the heckler was thrown out
news.author: Helena Vesty

news.title: US Judge Extends Curbs On Trump's Golf Course Project After 400 Trees Cut
news.text: A federal judge agreed Monday to extend an order blocking the Trump administration's renovation plans for a century-old public golf course in the nation's capital.US District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction that temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" to the course while the lawsuit is active."The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees.' The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law," Reyes wrote.Reyes expressed astonishment that the government has asked her to "not to believe the sitting President" and disregard Trump's statements about his plans for the golf course renovations."This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."On October 18, Trump announced plans on social media to close the golf course for 15 months, starting November 15, and redevelop the 106-year-old park and course despite a court challenge by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. A day later, Trump posted that the work would start immediately.Reyes, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Joe Biden, previously ordered the administration to suspend work on the project until at least October 26.The plaintiffs challenging the project claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. At a hearing, the judge excoriated the government after workers cut down at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend with little notice to the plaintiffs.The course renovation project is part of the Republican president's aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington's historic landscape, including his plans to construct a huge ballroom at the White House, to build a massive arch and to add his own name to the Kennedy Center.Reyes rejected the administration's request for her to recuse herself from the case. The government questioned her impartiality and accused her of engaging in "egregious" behavior from the bench during an emergency hearing in the case.In Monday's ruling Reyes stressed that she had hoped the parties could have resolved their dispute without judicial intervention. She noted that she had denied plaintiffs' previous requests."The Court would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once-ler redux. Indeed, for months, the Court declined to intervene," she wrote.But she said the government forced her hand by bulldozing hundreds of trees without any notice, doing "what it assured all it would not do."Democracy Forward President & CEO Skye Perryman, whose organization is co-counsel representing the plaintiffs, DC Preservation League and two golfers, called the ruling "a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm." She added, in an email, that the move will stop activities "while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court."The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: At a hearing, the judge excoriated the government after workers cut down at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend with little notice to the plaintiffs.

 Sinclair rejects claims that plea bargaining absent from Firearms Act 







Government Senator Charles Sinclair says a narrative created by some individuals in the legal fraternity that no provision exists for plea bargain under the current Firearms Act is inaccurate and misleading.

“What I find interesting is that no one appears to have spoken about the possibility of using the Plea Negotiation and Agreements Act in order to achieve for their client reduce sentence below the minimum mandatory,” Senator Sinclair, a prominent defence attorney, told journalists on Monday.

“The 2022 legislation made a consequential amendment to the Plea Negotiation and Agreements Act and included in particular, I mean section 5, a provision which would be described as section 5.2a, whereby there can be pre negotiations done with the CROW and for persons to receive a sentence below the minimum mandatory of 15 years,” he added. 

On page 130 of the Act, Section 5(2a) says in the case of an offence under the Act, a plea bargain arrangement may be accessed if there is the provision of information that assists the Crown in the prevention, detection or investigation of, or in proceedings relating to, the offence concerned or any other offence.

Senator Sinclair says there is precedent for an accused successfully using that section of the law to obtain a reduced sentence.

“I am fully aware that this particular amendment was used successfully in the gun court in relation to a person who was charged with possession simpliciter, andthat person received, by virtue of the plea agreement that was done and the agreement of the judge, obviously, at the end of the day, received a sentence significantly below the minimum mandatory sentence of 15 years,” Senator Sinclair said. 

He made the comments against the background of renewed concerns being expressed by lawyers over the Act following the recommendation by the National Security Council (NSC) that individuals convicted of illegal possession of a firearm should face a new minimum mandatory sentence of 20 years imprisonment.

Senator Sinclair says there may be a lack of awareness in the legal field about provisions of the law which allow for pleas bargain arrangements.

“So, whilst the discussion is taking place in relation to the minimum of 15 years, which potentially, having regard to the comments, can be increased to 20 years in the event that there is an amendment to the 2022 legislation, the possibility still exists for a lesser sentence by virtue of plea negotiations, and I would encourage persons to look at it and to seek to use it in moving forward,” Sinclair further commented.

news.title: Trump, Iran, Economy: 5 Big Issues Shaping US Midterms
news.text: Americans voting in the November 3 midterm elections will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency, along with dozens of governorships and thousands of state offices.The campaign is playing out against an unusually combustible mix of economic anxiety, war, immigration battles, corruption concerns and unease over rapidly expanding artificial intelligence.Polls asking voters about priorities use different methodologies, but they broadly agree on the dominance of pocketbook concerns.An October Pew survey found economic issues easily topped voters' worries, while a September Emerson poll put the Iran war, jobs, tariffs, gas prices, immigration and AI regulation among the most important factors in voting decisions.Here are five issues shaping the midterms:It's The EconomyAffordability remains issue number one.Inflation was running at 3.7 percent in September, but the political problem goes beyond the headline rate, with voters paying more for gasoline, housing, electricity, groceries and borrowing.Pew found that 65 percent of Americans see Trump's economic policies as hurtful to the economy.Another survey, from the Joseph Rainey Center for Public Policy, found 57 percent placing groceries, gas or utilities among their top three issues.Trump's tariffs feed directly into the debate, with opponents blaming them for higher costs while the administration argues they protect American industry and raise revenue.Iran WarA foreign war has become a domestic pocketbook issue.The conflict with Iran, underway since February, has driven energy costs higher and become deeply unpopular.Emerson's September survey rated the Iran war the single most important issue among those it tested, while Reuters/Ipsos found only 34 percent approving of Trump's handling of the conflict.Republican candidates in several competitive races have called for the fighting to end, and four Republican senators joined Democrats in a September vote seeking to rein it in.ImmigrationThe strength of Trump's signature political talking point has become more complicated.The president returned to office promising mass deportations, but support has eroded following controversy over deaths during arrests and detention, and aggressive ICE operations.Reuters/Ipsos found 55 percent disapproved of Trump's handling of immigration. Marist, meanwhile, found Democrats and Republicans essentially level on which party voters trusted more on the issue -- a striking change from the clear Republican advantage of 2024.The shift is particularly notable among Latinos. A survey across competitive House districts found 62 percent of Latino voters disapproved of the administration's deportation and immigration enforcement.Trump, Money And PowerThe president himself is an issue -- including how he uses the office.Trump has explicitly asked voters to behave as though he were on the ballot, making the election partly a referendum on his second term.Government ethics ranked second behind the economy in Pew's open-ended survey, cited by nine percent of voters.A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found 97 percent of Americans believed there was at least some corruption in the federal government. And 66 percent said they had little or no trust in Trump to avoid using the presidency to benefit his family's businesses.Democrats have promised investigations of Trump family business dealings if they win congressional subpoena power, although Republicans dismiss many such allegations as partisan attacks.AI Comes To TownArtificial intelligence has jumped out of the laptop and onto the campaign trail.Voters worry about job losses, safety and regulation -- but increasingly also about the giant data centers needed to power AI.Half of Americans told Pew they were very concerned about AI's role in the economy, while 59 percent said they disliked political leaders supporting data centers in the respondents' localities.AI regulation scored surprisingly highly in Emerson's September survey, just behind immigration and gas prices. Data centers themselves ranked lower nationally, but have become major campaign issues in states including Ohio as communities battle over electricity, water and construction.Congress even spent some of its final pre-election days arguing over who should pay the electricity costs created by them -- proof that, in 2026, even the server farm has become political.READ | Trump Pledges $1 Million For Information Leading To Vote Fraud ConvictionOther Fault LinesNot every familiar American culture-war issue has dominated the 2026 campaign, but several remain potent dividing lines.Transgender rights continue to produce fierce arguments over participation in women's sports. Health care is also a perennial election concern, encompassing the cost of insurance and medicines, and access to coverage.These issues have not necessarily driven the national midterm campaign as strongly as affordability, Iran or immigration, but they remain powerful mobilizers for parts of both parties' coalitions.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: The conflict with Iran, underway since February, has driven energy costs higher and become deeply unpopular.

news.title: Week from midterm election, polls project grim prospect for Trump
news.text: Digital Desk | New York, Oct 27 (IANS) A week before midterm elections, polls project grim prospects for President Donald Trump, who is weighed down by the economic fallout of his tariff war and the Iran conflict on US voters. The consensus among major poll analysts is that his Republican Party will lose control of the House of Representatives while the Senate outcome is hovering in the realm of a toss-up. Trump's next two years in office will depend on which party controls either chamber of Congress or both. If Democrats control either, they can try to obstruct his policies and actions, or Trump can vehemently defy them, a standoff that could bring judicial intervention. At the very least, the US could see a replay of his first term when the Democrat-controlled House impeached him -- and he warned his supporters could happen again. Signs of his desperation are his offer of $5,000 to every American adult if the Republicans win the midterms, and not only lifting sanctions placed on Russia for its Ukraine invasion -- after having imposed a 100 per cent tariff on India at one time -- but also entering into a deal with Russia's President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel. Trump has declared the midterms a referendum on the first 20 months of his second administration, telling citizens to vote as if he was on the ballot, even though many Republicans are distancing themselves from him because of his low ratings. Republican New Hampshire Senate candidate John Sununu, for example, said in an ad, “When the president’s policies are bad for New Hampshire, I’ll oppose them, just like I opposed the war in Iran and the trade war with Canada". Trump seems to have admitted the popularity of his party -- and him -- is dimming even in their electoral fortresses, by concentrating his campaign in the reliably red states that he carried in the presidential election in order to shore up support for Republican candidates, rather than take the battle to blue states to topple Democrats. "Every single place I go, people that are down are now winning", he asserted recently about his “Trumpapaloozas”, the rallies he is holding from Alaska in the north to Texas in the South. And his Justice Department has taken the unusual step of filing a case to stop the Senate election in Alaska officially declared if the Republican candidate Dan S. Sullivan loses, because, the Trump administration says, there is another candidate with a similar name, Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot, and it confuses voters. The voting is already in progress, and as of Monday, nearly 30 million citizens had voted either through postal ballots or at in-person early voting stations. There are 217 million registered voters, and the turnout in midterm election is usually low, recording 46.2 per cent in 2022 and 50 per cent in 2018. Democrats flipping the House majority would be in line with the historical trend of the president's party losing the midterms, but the size of the majority would matter. RealClear Politics (RCP), which aggregates polls, reported that only 38.2 per cent of likely voters approve of Trump's job performance, while 60.2 per cent disapprove of Trump job. And, tellingly, 57 per cent say Trump policies are making them financially worse off. That would echo worldwide sentiments about the impacts of the Iran conflict that Trump launched alongside Israel, and the tariff war, but hit closer to home for Trump. The inflation rate was 3.7 per cent last month (up from 3.4 per cent in August), but it bites consumers much harder than would be expected due to the soaring prices of petroleum, especially diesel, and its multiplier effect on food and other items of daily use, as well as the impact of tariffs on many items of everyday use. This stings because during the 2024 election campaign, he had boasted he would bring down the price of petrol to $2 a gallon (53 cents per litre), but now the average price is $4.28 a gallon ($1.13 per litre), and diesel is $6.28 a gallon ($1.66 per litre). In this scenario, RCP gave Democrats a majority with 227 seats in the 435-member House, even with 25 seats it put in the "toss-up category" where neither party has a clear lead and can go either way. Cook Political Report, an authoritative source for non-partisan analysis, projects 220 seats for Democrats, with 17 tossups. Its editor for House elections, Erin Covey, was forthright about the outcome: "Republicans’ path to keeping control of the House has all but evaporated". CBS News said Democrats could get 229 seats for Democrats and Republicans 206, with the caveat because of previous polls being off the mark: "Republicans do still have a very narrow path to hold the majority, too". That's because, according to CBS News, "There isn't a growing [Democratic] wave" and "the still undecided or uncertain voters tend to profile as more Republican". news.title: Judge continues to block Trump from cutting down trees at D.C. golf course
news.text: A federal judge on Monday barred the Trump administration from removing trees from East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., in a colorful ruling that follows a weekslong controversy over President Trump's plans to overhaul the publicly owned course."The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."In a 70-page preliminary injunction ruling, Reyes prohibited the government from "removing or damaging" any trees on the golf course while a lawsuit challenging the renovation plan works its way through the court system. The judge also required 10 days' notice before the government makes "any irreparable modification" to the course.The judge had previously blocked tree removal through Monday.Mr. Trump has sought to overhaul the golf course — which sits beside the Potomac River — for months, pitching a "World Class Championship Golf Course" fit to host high-profile professional tournaments instead of the current "dysfunctional" course. The D.C. Preservation League sued over the planned changes to the course, arguing the government violated the National Environmental Policy Act by failing to analyze the project's impacts.Reyes has sparred with the government since it cut down hundreds of trees earlier this month with little notice to the court or plaintiffs. In a hearing two weeks ago, after more than 430 trees were felled, the judge told lawyers for the government that they had "lost credibility," and she was "furious" and "thoroughly unamused."Mr. Trump said last week the course would close for construction beginning in November, and it would reopen in 15 months. He later said work would begin "IMMEDIATELY."In her ruling Monday, Reyes argued Mr. Trump's statements about the renovation plans were tough to square with government lawyers' position that it's legally too early to challenge the plans in court because there was no final decision."Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President," she wrote. "This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more. It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."Reyes said she was initially reluctant to intervene in the case, writing that she "would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux" — a reference to an earlier court hearing in which Reyes invoked the Dr. Seuss character to explain why she wasn't interested in micromanaging the federal government's tree management efforts.She said she only intervened "because the Government did what it assured all it would not do," by chopping down hundreds of trees on the golf course.Reyes found that the D.C. Preservation League is likely to succeed in showing the Trump administration's plans for the golf course violate the legal requirement for an environmental review.She also found that the tree-cutting efforts were part of the renovation plan. The judge said she did not find statements by the Department of Interior's deputy chief of staff to be credible, including his description of the agency's tree management plan as "cleaning up" the course.CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and the Department of Interior for comment.Mr. Trump has feuded with Reyes, calling her a "crazed lunatic."Earlier this month, the Trump administration asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case, arguing that she had shown "open hostility" to the government and that her "histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial.""To name just a few examples of bias, Judge Reyes has unfairly questioned Trump Administration attorneys' intelligence, allowed her disdain for the Trump Administration to influence how hearings unfold, and systematically disregarded basic separation of powers principles and Article III constraints on judicial authority," government attorneys wrote.Reyes rejected that request and denied that she is biased, listing out compliments that she has paid government lawyers."So what happened? Not sudden onset bias," Reyes wrote in her denial. "Instead, the Government decided to remove over 500 healthy, non-invasive trees from East Potomac Golf Course. It waited until 4:55 p.m. on the Friday of a holiday weekend to give notice that it would begin removing trees within 15 hours. It removed nearly 430 trees in one day and would have destroyed hundreds more but for a rain delay."
news.summary: "The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

news.title: Left In Brazil
news.text:
Brazil has come as a surprise at a time when extreme Right parties in Europe, Latin America and elsewhere, helped and encouraged by US President Donald Trump, had been on a winning streak. Brazil’s veteran Left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva recorded a historic win beating his Right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro.

The victory came when defeat was staring Lula in the face. After trailing behind his rival in the earlier vote, he succeeded in securing 51.79 per cent of the votes, compared with Bolsonaro’s 48.21 per cent in the run-off polls.

As could be expected, Bolsonaro, like his father in 2022, refused to accept the result citing the extension of polling time by two hours as “inexplicable” even though both the parties had requested that polling stations be kept open longer for different reasons. Bolsonaro told his supporters in Brasilia that he would seek the annulment of the election.

It is Lula’s fourth win in a presidential election, having served two terms as President from January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023. Bolsonaro had beaten Lula in the first round on 4 October and it appeared virtually impossible for Lula to turn the result around in just three weeks. The victory reverses the trend across Latin America where Right and conservative forces recently took control of one country after another such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia.

Since his defeat in the first round, Lula spared no pains to mobilise Left and democratic supporters through street demonstrations and a massive social media push. He had been facing a hostile Trump administration though the US President did not directly endorse Lula’s rival unlike what he did with the Right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections held in Colombia and Honduras.

Undoubtedly, the Trump administration would have preferred to see a conservative at the helm of this massive country of 213 million people. Sensing this possibility, Lula had warned the US not to interfere with his country’s election.

It has been the strategy of the White House to spread its influence in Latin America so as to get support to its policies, including on defence, security and trade. It is also keen to reduce China’s influence in the Western Hemisphere.

Brazil, which is oil-rich and holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only big country in South America not governed by a Right-wing leader, while Lula is largely seen as China-friendly. Flavio Bolsonaro, in contrast, had promised to make Brazil a close ally of Washington. Lula’s victory is also good news for environmentalists who had feared that a win by Bolsonaro would have given Brazil’s influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power.

They remembered and were concerned over record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during the presidency of his father, Jair Bolsonaro. Despite Lula’s remarkable victory the results show how deeply divided the Brazilian population is with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro.

He would also have to confront the most Right-wing Congress in Brazil’s democratic era. This is the reason why Lula sounded a conciliatory tone at the hour of victory.

He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil’s opposing political poles with “a new way of governing.” However, he did not provide any detail as to how he would look after the interests of both his supporters and rivals.

Credit goes to Lula, who was once a factory worker and trade union leader, for rousing most of his Left supporters to go to the polling stations and cast their votes so that the Rightist forces could not assume the reins of power.

The working class responded well by turning out in large numbers. The message that Lula and his party drove home was that the return of autocratic forces in Brazil would spell doom for democracy. The victory could dampen the spirit of autocrats and anti-democratic parties across the globe.

news.title: Ex-FBI director James Comey 'facing criminal charges' over 'sensitive' data leaks
news.text: Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for allegedly leaking sensitive national defence information, according to reports. The former FBI director was charged on Monday with two counts for the alleged leak of sensitive information to the New York Times, the New York Post reports . These latest counts mark the third time the Department of Justice has pursued legal action against Mr Comey since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term in office. Prosecutors accuse Mr Comey of “knowingly and wittingly” transmitting national defence information as well as conspiring to do so in a “criminal information” filing made in the US District Court for the District of Columbia. The allegations cover a period from October 4 to 5, 2016. Mr Comey “through one and more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication” in violation of federal law, according to prosecutors. The new charges stem from an article in the New York Times on October 5, 2016, headlined “Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance by Adapting Spam Filter,” written by reporter Charlie Savage. “The United States’ investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” Special Assistant US Attorney Dustin Farahnak wrote in a filing, according to NBC News. “The investigation has uncovered evidence that Mr Comey directed staff to speak to Mr Savage about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.” The alleged sharing of information happened while Mr Comey was head of the FBI under President Barack Obama . Mr Comey was dismissed by President Trump in May 2017. “Well, they’re back, again,” Comey said in a video posted on his Substack, reported by the New York Post. “It would almost be funny if it wasn’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.” “Nothing’s changed with me,” the former FBI chief added. “I’m still innocent, and I’m still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent judiciary.” The case was filed under seal by the United States Department of Justice on October 5, 2026, and made public after Mr Comey’s lawyers filed a motion to unseal it. The former FBI director's attorneys have also asked the court to dismiss the case. A Justice Department spokesperson told The New York Post that the Department of Justice “filed a waiverless criminal information to toll the statute of limitations as it relates to allegations concerning former FBI Director Comey.” “Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals,” the spokesperson continued. “This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further.” The new charges against Mr Comey surfaced on the same day a US district judge ruled that the former FBI director’s daughter, Maurene Comey, was illegally fired from the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York last year, reports add. The judge ordered the Trump administration to reinstate Maurene Comey and provide her with back pay. James Comey was indicted by a federal grand jury last September on charges of making false statements and obstruction of justice. The case was dismissed after a judge ruled Lindsey Halligan, then US attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, was unlawfully appointed. The former FBI director was indicted again in April on charges of threatening to kill Trump in May 2025 when he posted a photograph on Instagram of seashells arranged to read “8647.” Mr Comey is still awaiting trial in the seashell case.
news.summary: These latest counts mark the third time the United States Department of Justice has pursued legal action against President Barack Obama's FBI director since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term in office
news.author: Helena Vesty

news.title: US-EU trade truce at risk over $3.4 billion Airbus loan, Trump official warns
news.text:
A tariff truce between the European Union and United States is potentially at risk due to a multibillion-dollar loan approved by the bloc's investment bank for Airbus this summer, President Donald Trump's top trade official said Monday. 

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer expressed concern that his office had received "no details about this loan" and pressed for the situation to be "resolved as soon as possible." 

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," Greer said in a statement. 

"This situation injects substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector," he continued.

In June, the European Investment Bank (EIB) said it would provide Airbus with a record three billion euros ($3.4 billion) in financing to boost its research and development.

Read moreFCAS project failure: 'France, Germany characterised by totally different strategic cultures'

"This new financing -- unprecedented in the EIB's history -- aims to provide Airbus with not only the capacity but also the flexibility needed to invest in long-term research, development and innovation across both commercial aviation and the security and defence sectors," EIB vice president Ambroise Fayolle told AFP at the time.

The United States and European Union had been squabbling over alleged unfair trade practices since 2004, with both sides claiming the other provided support to private companies, such as aircraft manufacturers Boeing and Airbus, in violation of international trade agreements. 

The 17-year-long feud saw the United States and EU impose tariffs on billions of dollars worth of each other's products. 

But in 2021, a five-year deal was agreed between both sides under former president Joe Biden's administration.

Both sides have not reimposed the tariffs since.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
news.summary: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer warned on Monday that a $3.4 billion European Investment Bank loan to Airbus could jeopardise a tariff truce between Washington and Brussels. Greer said his office had received no details about the financing, announced in June, and urged the EU to resolve the matter quickly.

news.title: Trump Judge Humiliates Him Week Before Midterms
news.text:
President Donald Trump has been humiliated just eight days away from the critical midterm elections by a judge he appointed.

On Monday, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the Trump administration, which made a last-minute attempt to block California from counting mail ballots cast by 20,000 registered voters they claim are noncitizens.

In a 2-1 decision, the court said it lacked jurisdiction over the appeal and granted a motion by Los Angeles County to dismiss the effort. The midterm elections are held on November 3.

The majority was joined by Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, who ⁠was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden. Judge Patrick Bumatay, another Trump appointee, dissented and said he would have granted the request. 

Bennett, who was nominated by Trump in 2018, and Sanchez ruled that the appeals court was not authorized to rule on the Department of Justice’s lawsuit before the district court had addressed it.

“The United States failed to allow the district court adequate opportunity to consider its application for a Temporary Restraining Order,” the majority wrote, as reported by Politico. “The United States’s claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one.”

Bennett and Sanchez also called out the Justice Department for waiting to file its lawsuit only three weeks ahead of the midterms, and only seeking the temporary restraining order from the district court last week, as ballots were already being processed.

They said it failed to allow a federal district court “adequate opportunity” to consider its request for temporary relief. 

As part of his dissent, Bumatay noted that the Trump administration’s belief that a federal criminal law to halt voting by noncitizens overruled California’s own electoral procedures would be likely to prevail. He claimed every day without action from the courts on the issue would boost the chances of votes by noncitizens being counted in the midterm elections. 

In a separate concurrence, in which Bennett rebutted Bumatay’s dissent, Bennett he said that the Trump administration “has offered no workable plan of any kind as to how the remedy it seeks could be accomplished in practice without potential catastrophic consequences to California’s ongoing election.” 

California Governor Gavin Newsom reacted to the ruling, claiming the Trump administration was trying to “baselessly sow doubt” over a state’s right to oversee elections within its own jurisdiction.

“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” Newsom said in a statement. “I have been sounding the alarm since last year, when Trump illegally federalized the California National Guard — Trump is illegally trying to seize powers in the Constitution entrusted to others so he can stay in power. This lawsuit is just the latest step.”

Newsom also warned, “Make no mistake: Trump’s assault on democracy won’t slow down... If everyone who cares about democracy participates, this election won’t be close — and none of Trump’s lies or conspiracy theories will be able to call that result, and the will of people, into doubt.”

A hearing in the case is now scheduled for Tuesday in the U.S. District Court in California.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House and the Justice Department for comment.
news.summary:
Jonathan Ernst / REUTERSPresident Donald Trump has been humiliated just eight days away from the critical midterm elections by a judge he appointed.

On Monday, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the Trump administration, which made a last-minute attempt to block California from counting mail ballots cast by 20,000 registered voters they claim are noncitizens.

In a 2-1 decision, the court said it lacked jurisdiction over the appeal and granted a motion by Los Angeles County to dismiss the effort. The midterm elections are held on November 3.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Trump announces $1 million reward for voter fraud tips ahead of midterms
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 27 (IANS) President Donald Trump has said he will offer a $1 million reward to anyone who reports voter fraud that leads to an arrest and conviction, days before the November 3 midterm elections. Speaking to reporters on Monday before boarding Air Force One, Trump also said his administration was “starting that process” on deporting non-citizens who vote. “I’m also going to be issuing $1 million bonus or reward or whatever you want to call it, for anybody that reports voter fraud, leading to the arrest and conviction of somebody. We’re giving that person $1 million,” Trump said. A reporter told the President that he had “made it very clear that any non-citizen that votes would be automatically deported,” and asked whether that would “clean up elections” and whether he should say so at all his rallies. “Well, I think so. And we do that and we’re starting that process,” Trump replied. The White House has not released details of how the reward would be paid, which agency would administer it, or what legal authority it would rest on. Voting by non-citizens in federal elections is already a federal crime. Under existing law, it can lead to fines, imprisonment and removal from the country. The remarks are expected to draw attention from immigrant communities, including the large number of Indian nationals living in the US on green cards and temporary work visas. They are not eligible to vote in federal elections. Community groups have previously voiced concern that aggressive voter-roll checks could wrongly flag naturalised citizens. The announcement comes as Trump steps up his campaign travel before the midterms. He is scheduled to hold rallies in Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, while Vice President JD Vance campaigns in Howell, Michigan. Trump has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections, and his remarks on Monday also touched on elections abroad. He said the vote count in Brazil “had a very bad look.” On Israel, he defended issuing two endorsements in its election. Democrats have accused the administration of using law enforcement to intimidate voters ahead of the polls. Election officials in several states have said cases of non-citizen voting are rare. The midterm elections will decide control of the House of Representatives and a third of the Senate, and several Indian American candidates are on the ballot across the country.

news.title: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
news.text:
Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing. 

It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.

Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.

Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".

"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.

"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.

This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.

Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration. 

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said. 

The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".

His legal team has filed a motion to dismiss the charges.

Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC that the case may have exceeded the 10-year statute of limitations, giving the motion to dismiss the charges "a very good chance of being granted".

Kirschner said it seemed like the charges against Comey were a "revenge-fuelled attempt by Donald Trump to have his Department of Justice find something that might stick".
news.summary: Comey's lawyers say the case stems from alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in 2016.
news.author: Sareen Habeshian

news.title: Trump calls Obama 'lousy president' over 'Cheesecake Factory' jibe on White House makeover
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 27 (IANS) President Donald Trump has hit back at former President Barack Obama for comparing the renovated White House to the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain, calling him “not smart at all” and a “lousy president.” Speaking to reporters on Monday before boarding Air Force One, Trump was asked about Obama having “made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, uh, comparing it to the White House, in your decorations.” “No. You know, I’ve taken care of the White House. I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world. We have reskinned it. It was in horrible shape,” Trump said. He said many ornaments on the building “were missing or damaged or gone for a long time,” and that “the exterior plaster was broken, cracked. The painting was terrible.” “The White House is now in the best shape it’s been since 1792, when it was built,” Trump said. He then turned on his predecessor. “Guys like Obama, they would pass the front door. They’d see the broken masonry,” Trump said. He added that Obama “wouldn’t notice because he doesn’t notice that. He doesn’t notice dirt and filth.” “We have to explain that to Obama because he doesn’t understand it, because he’s not a smart guy. Let me tell you, in my opinion, he’s not smart at all,” Trump said. “Because the way he ran the country, only a stupid person would run the country like that.” Trump said the work had been done by “very talented people,” many of them from the Department of the Interior, at “very little money spent.” “So we took molds of the one side and we put it on the other side, and we did a beautiful job,” he said. “It’s not about money, it’s about seeing.” He ended with a direct rebuke. “And for you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” Trump said. The exchange comes as Obama has been campaigning for Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Trump’s renovations of the White House have drawn criticism from Democrats and preservation groups over cost and transparency. At the same appearance, Trump announced a $1 million reward for anyone reporting voter fraud that leads to an arrest and conviction, and commented on elections in Brazil and Israel. Obama’s office did not immediately respond to Trump’s remarks.

news.title: Israel goes to polls with war, security and Netanyahu's future at stake
news.text:
Israelis are heading to the polls on Tuesday to elect all 120 members of the country's parliament, the Knesset, in a closely watched election that could determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power or the opposition succeeds in forming a new government.
The election is taking place amid ongoing security concerns following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, subsequent regional conflicts and domestic disagreements over the government's policies. The outcome will shape Israel's political direction, security priorities and approach to governance.
Voting begins at 7 am local time in Israel, or 9:30 am India time. Most polling stations are scheduled to remain open until 10 pm local time, which is 12:30 am on October 28 in India. Exit polls are expected after voting ends, offering an initial indication of the possible outcome.
Netanyahu faces a crucial test
The election pits Netanyahu's right-wing Likud-led coalition against opposition parties seeking to change the country's leadership and political direction.
Netanyahu, one of Israel's longest-serving prime ministers, faces scrutiny over his government's handling of national security, the wars and conflicts involving Israel, and domestic political divisions.
The vote will also test the support for parties and leaders offering alternatives to the current government. However, the outcome will depend not only on which party receives the most votes but also on which political groups can secure enough parliamentary seats to form a governing coalition.
 The Prime Minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu (C) speaks at Ben Yehuda Market during a campaign visit in Jerusalem on October 22, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Photo by JOHN WESSELS / AFP)
Security, military service and judicial reforms dominate debate
Israel's election campaign has been shaped by questions over national security, military accountability, compulsory service and the balance of power between the government and the judiciary.
National security remains a central concern following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the conflicts that followed. Voters are weighing the government's response to the attacks, its handling of the war and its broader regional strategy, including its approach towards Iran.
Another major point of contention is military conscription. Most ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, known as Haredim, have historically received exemptions from compulsory military service while studying in religious seminaries. The issue has become more pressing as Israel faces military manpower shortages and repeated reserve mobilisations following years of conflict.
Judicial reform and the independence of state institutions form another key part of the political contest. Netanyahu's proposed judicial overhaul in 2023 triggered mass protests over concerns that it would weaken the judiciary and limit checks on executive power. Opposition parties have pledged to reverse the changes and strengthen institutional accountability, while Netanyahu and his allies argue that reforms are needed to rebalance power between elected representatives and the courts.
The cost of living is also weighing on voters, as rising prices and increased defence spending add to economic pressures.
Who is Netanyahu's main challenger? Enter Gadi Eisenkot
Gadi Eisenkot, 66, spent more than four decades in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), serving as its chief of general staff from 2015 to 2019. He is associated with the military strategy known as the ‘Dahiya doctrine’, which involves the use of overwhelming force against adversaries.
Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Eisenkot joined Benjamin Netanyahu’s war cabinet as an observer alongside Benny Gantz. He later resigned, accusing Netanyahu of putting political survival ahead of a clear post-war plan and efforts to secure a hostage deal.
As leader of the centrist Yashar party, Eisenkot has called for an independent state inquiry into the October 7 failures and equal military or national service obligations, opposing exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews. On Iran, he advocates coordination with international allies and cautions against using military operations for domestic political gain. He is seeking to unite opposition parties into a broad coalition to challenge Netanyahu’s government.
 Gadi Eisenkot, Israel's former military chief of staff and leader of the Yashar party, addresses supporters at the party's final campaign rally before the legislative election, in Tel Aviv on October 25, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Photo by Jack GUEZ / AFP)
Iran war adds to election stakes
The war between Israel, the United States and Iran has emerged as a major issue ahead of the election, with the outcome potentially influencing the direction of Israel's security policy and its approach to Tehran.
The United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, triggering Iranian attacks on Israel and Gulf states. Although direct exchanges of fire between Israel and Iran have been suspended since June, tensions remain high, with concerns over a possible resumption of hostilities.
Netanyahu has argued for a hardline approach towards Iran, calling for Israel to prioritise military action to prevent emerging threats. His political opponents have also emphasised national security, but differences remain over how aggressively Israel should pursue its objectives and whether greater emphasis should be placed on diplomacy.
 A bus bearing a campaign poster featuring Israeli Prime Minister and Likud party chairman Benjamin Netanyahu alongside US President Donald Trump drives through Jerusalem on October 26, 2026, on the eve of Israel's legislative elections. (Photo by AHMAD GHARABLI / AFP)
How Israel's electoral system works
Israel uses a system of proportional representation in which voters choose political parties rather than directly electing a prime minister.
The country is divided into a single nationwide constituency for parliamentary elections. Parties receive seats broadly in proportion to their share of the vote, provided they cross the 3.25 per cent electoral threshold.
A party does not need to win an outright majority to participate in government. Instead, parties typically negotiate with other groups to build a coalition that commands the support of at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 members.
This means that even a party finishing first in the election may struggle to form a government if it cannot secure support from enough other parties. Coalition negotiations can therefore play a decisive role in determining who becomes prime minister.
When will the results be announced?
Initial indications of the outcome are expected after polling stations close, when Israeli broadcasters release exit polls.
The counting process and subsequent coalition negotiations could take several days or longer, depending on how fragmented the results are.
Israel's Central Elections Committee is scheduled to publish the official results by November 4. President Isaac Herzog will then consult political parties and nominate a candidate considered most likely to form a government. The nominee can have up to 42 days to assemble a coalition.

news.title: Now home, Venezuela opposition leader Machado walks tightrope with supporters and Trump
news.text: CARACAS/BOGOTA - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned on Sunday after nearly a year away, will walk a tightrope as she seeks the elections her supporters want without running afoul of a U.S.-backed negotiation process between the interim government and other opposition groups.Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. Washington has said she has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.The talks, which have continued this month, would remake the electoral council and top court ahead of eventual elections. Both bodies are staffed by ruling party loyalists and backed ousted President Nicolas Maduro in a disputed 2024 presidential election, despite tallies published by Machado’s movement that showed her candidate had won. The U.S. military captured Maduro in January.
news.summary: Machado's return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.

news.title: Trump’s approval ratings slightly recover after record low last week: Report
news.text: US President Donald Trump’s public approval rating rose by one percentage point to 32 per cent, a slight recovery from last week’s record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.Trump’s Republican Party is fighting to keep control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.In the five-day nationwide poll, registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans by 47 per cent to 36 per cent when asked which party they would back for Congress. This 11-point gap was one percentage point smaller than in the previous Reuters/Ipsos poll, which closed on October 19.When undecided voters were asked which party they were leaning towards, the Democratic lead shrank further to nine percentage points, with 50 per cent favouring Democrats and 41 per cent Republicans.Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda during the last two years of his second term, Reuters reported.The poll also pointed to a change in voters’ views on economic management. Reuters/Ipsos surveys beforethe war had shown voters preferring Republicans over Democrats on the economy. In the latest poll, 37 per cent of voters said Democrats had a better approach to the economy, against 33 per cent who favoured Republicans.Democratic voters also reported more enthusiasm about the midterms. About 46 per cent of Democrats said they were very enthusiastic about voting, compared with 30 per cent of Republicans.Generic ballot polls show which party voters would prefer to control Congress nationwide. However, they do not show how individual states and constituencies are likely to vote, which ultimately determines control of the House and Senate. Republicans have some structural advantages in these local contests, Reuters reported.The online Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters. The margin of error was two percentage points for all adults and three percentage points for registered voters.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump’s approval rating has increased to 32 percent, showing a small recovery. In contrast, a recent poll indicates that registered voters prefer Democrats over Republicans by 47 percent to 36 percent. As the midterm elections approach, voter enthusiasm appears to be higher among Democrats compared to Republicans. Additionally, voters’ views on economic management have shifted, favoring Democrats slightly over Republicans.

news.title: US lawmakers warn banks, ports against Russian diesel as Trump defends energy dealings with Moscow
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 27 (IANS) A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has warned the chief executives of major American banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that importing Russian diesel could expose them to criminal and civil liability, as President Donald Trump defended his energy dealings with Moscow. The letters were sent on Saturday by Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons, Elizabeth Warren and Republican Thom Tillis, along with Congressman Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee released them on Monday. “Any importation of Russian diesel into the U.S. raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations. Companies that import products in violation of U.S. law may expose themselves to both criminal and civil liability,” the lawmakers wrote. The letters went to the CEOs of JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo Bank, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, and to the heads of the port authorities of Houston, Corpus Christi and Beaumont in Texas and of New York/New Jersey. The lawmakers cited Trump’s October 9 announcement and the Treasury Department’s General License 135. They said the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 generally bars Russian energy imports unless the President certifies to Congress that Russia has ceased hostilities in Ukraine. “Granting Moscow the ability to freely sell Russian diesel in global markets damages America’s security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine,” they wrote. According to the release, public reporting and vessel tracking data show ships carrying Russian diesel are on track to reach Beaumont and New York/New Jersey as soon as the end of this month. The lawmakers asked the companies to preserve all related records and to confirm by October 28. Separately, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin has written to the oil industry warning against the arrangement, Politico reported. Trump, speaking to reporters on Sunday before boarding Air Force One, defended the move. “The only deal we made with Russia, frankly, they released oil into the world,” he said. He added, “we’re not gonna be hostage with the oil industry.” He also referred to special envoy Steve Witkoff’s trip to Moscow. The diesel issue is being watched closely in New Delhi. India became one of the largest buyers of Russian crude after the Ukraine war began, and US policy on Russian energy has been a sore point in the ongoing India-US trade negotiations. Washington had earlier imposed additional tariffs on India over its Russian oil purchases. [ The Treasury Department did not immediately respond to the lawmakers’ letters.

news.title: Can Netanyahu survive another storm? Israel votes after Oct 7, Gaza & Iran wars
news.text: Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a crucial test of his political future in Tuesday's election, with voters weighing his leadership following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, successive wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel's growing international isolation, news agency Reuters reported.Despite the mounting challenges, Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable political survivor. With nationalist politics firmly entrenched and the country's fragmented electoral system making coalition-building decisive, he could still emerge best placed to form the next government.Opinion polls point to a close contest between Netanyahu's Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk who has attracted support from both right-wing and centrist voters.Netanyahu has made his wartime leadership and close relationship with US President Donald Trump central to his campaign. Trump has endorsed the Israeli leader, with the two countries joining forces in the war against Iran.On Sunday, Netanyahu said Trump was prepared to act again to “finally” remove the Iranian threat, but only if he remained in power. Eisenkot, however, accused the prime minister of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats," adding that Trump would work "in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people."Netanyahu may once again need the support of far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to secure a governing majority. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries over allegations of inciting violence against Palestinians. Meanwhile, Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party has gained ground in opinion polls.Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear route to power. If neither manages to assemble a coalition in Israel's 120-member parliament, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker prime minister until another election is held next year.Polling stations are scheduled to remain open from 7 am to 10 pm (0500 to 2000 GMT).The October 7 reckoningThe election comes after one of the most turbulent periods in Israel's history since its establishment in 1948. The trauma of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, Israel's subsequent military offensive in Gaza and deep divisions over Netanyahu's right-wing government have dominated the country's political landscape.For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the vote is also a referendum on accountability for the security failures that preceded October 7, Israel's deadliest day.Mali Hajaj, an education ministry employee who supports Eisenkot, said a national inquiry into the attacks was essential for the country to begin healing."the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that's where our healing will come from," she said.Lisa Tortor, another voter opposed to Netanyahu, said she hoped he would leave office and a new government would begin repairing the damage to Israel's international standing and the wider Jewish community.She said she hoped Netanyahu would go and "they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel's image."Not all voters, however, believe the prime minister should be held responsible for the October 7 attacks. Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, dismissed that criticism and backed Netanyahu's leadership during the war.Gabay called him "the right man for the state of Israel" and said, "Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way."Netanyahu's wartime record under scrutinyThe election campaign has unfolded against the backdrop of years of military conflict that have reshaped Israel's security and diplomatic position.After the October 7 attacks, in which Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage, Israel launched a military offensive that devastated much of Gaza. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks have killed 74,000 people.Israel also dealt major blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and exchanged strikes with Iran before launching a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025. The conflict escalated further this year with a joint US-Israeli war against Iran.Netanyahu has presented his handling of these conflicts as evidence of his leadership and ability to confront Israel's security threats. His alliance with Trump has also become a key part of his pitch to voters, particularly as tensions with Iran remain central to the campaign.Eisenkot, meanwhile, has argued that Israel's next government must ensure Iran does not acquire a military nuclear capability. He has said this could be achieved through military action or an "arrangement", including a diplomatic solution backed by the United States.The competing positions underline how security policy remains central to the election, even as voters grapple with questions about accountability, the future of the Gaza conflict and Israel's standing abroad.Coalition arithmetic could decide the outcomeEven if Eisenkot's alliance makes gains, forming a government could prove difficult. Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, his camp opposes the two-state solution that has underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.Eisenkot has, however, criticised violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Such violence has surged since 2023, straining Israel's ties with Western countries. He has also opposed Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.Meanwhile, dissatisfaction with Netanyahu has prompted some voters in traditional Likud strongholds to campaign against him.
