news.title: Israel denies Netanyahu-army chief rift over Iran attack ahead of polls
news.text:
Defence minister rules out pre-election strike on Tehran; Israeli premier dismisses reports of clash with army chief
• Netanyahu pushed Trump to launch attack before Israel polls, CNN reports

JERUSALEM: Israeli Defe-nce Minister Israel Katz on Monday ruled out an attack on Iran before the election, dismissing reports of an “unprecedented confrontation” between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over Iran.

The reports originated on Sunday, when Israel’s Channel 12 reported the two men clashed over an unspecified directive concerning Iran ahead of Tues-day’s closely contested vote.

Zamir demanded legal guarantees and political leaders’ signatures before executing the order, amid fears that military action could provoke immediate confrontation with Tehran.

Netanyahu dismissed the report as “rubbish”, while Katz went further, saying that claims of gaps between the political leadership and the military were “entirely baseless and false”.

He characterised it as an eff-ort to cast doubt on the Netan-yahu bloc’s judgement on the eve of the polls saying “unequivocally that there was no intention on Israel’s part to initiate an attack on Iran before the elections”.

The denials came as CNN published a report casting the issue in a very different light.

Citing two US officials, the network said American forces in the Middle East were prepared to launch new, potentially major operations against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from Donald Trump.

According to the report, Neta-n-yahu had in fact been pushing for further strikes, while US officials urged Israel to wait until Washington was ready for joint action. “Netanyahu really wanted and tried to convince Trump for a joint attack in Iran before the elections, and Trump did not give a green light,” an Israeli security source told CNN.

Officials said an order could come before the end of the year, most likely after the US midterm elections on Nov. 3. Israel delayed immediate strike plans but is preparing for possible joint operations with the US after the midterms, CNN reported.

In Israel, the reports fed into an already heated campaign. Opposition figures accused Netanyahu of risking a wider conflict with Iran for political gain. Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief and Netanyahu’s principal rival, warned against drawing the military into electoral politics.

“I warn Netanyahu: do not dare place your political interests above the state’s security,” he wrote on X.

Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition politician, went a step further, saying he had asked the attorney general to investigate allegations that Netanyahu pressured security officials into actions that could provoke Iran.

news.title: Indian American Republicans signal 'buyer’s remorse' over anti-Indian rhetoric week before midterms
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 27 (IANS) A growing number of Indian American voters who backed Republicans in 2024 are signalling they may switch sides in the November 3 midterm elections, citing a rise in anti-Indian rhetoric within the conservative movement, according to new polling and community leaders. A recent survey commissioned by the advocacy group Indian American Impact found that a quarter of Indian Americans who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 planned to vote for Democrats in the midterms, US media reported. Democrats led Republicans among likely voters at around 66 per cent, while nearly two-thirds of Independent South Asian voters said they were undecided. "There are a large chunk of [Indian American] voters who are, for lack of a better word, having buyers remorse," Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, told local media. "That's something that is building across the community as we're talking about hate and discrimination.” The poll found that, like most voters, Indian Americans ranked the cost of living and healthcare as top issues. A February survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace found that seven in 10 Indian Americans disapproved of Trump's second-term performance, but also that just 46 per cent identified as Democrats, down from 2020, The Verge reported. About one-third of Indian Americans supported Trump in 2024. Anang Mittal, a longtime conservative strategist who previously worked for Senator Mitch McConnell, told The Verge that Republican politicians believe they can tolerate anti-Indian remarks because the community is small. An estimated 5.2 million Indian Americans live in the US, just over 1.5 per cent of the population. "They decided there's no price to be paid when it comes to engaging in language that treats Indian immigrants as outsiders and not compatible with American culture," Mittal said. In Texas, home to the country's most expensive Senate race, community leaders said the shift is visible. "I've seen a few people who say they're just going to vote Democrat straight down the ballot, to send a message to the Republican Party that they're not going to tolerate it," Rishi Bhutada, a Houston businessman and board member of the Hindu American Foundation said. The rhetoric has included a post by Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, about South Asian fans at a University of Texas football game, which Governor Greg Abbott said was "not my message." Conservative commentator Chris Rufo also hosted a podcast episode titled "The Indian Question.” Community leaders have linked the online climate to recent incidents, including an alleged plot to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, and the stabbing of Sikh truck driver Gurvinder Singh in Wyoming. "We could have been talking about a massive tragedy," Patel said of the Illinois case. One US media outlet said districts with significant Indian American populations include New Jersey's 7th and Pennsylvania's 1st, both Democratic pick-up targets, as well as swing states Georgia and Michigan. On Monday, Indian American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi said he was leading "256 bipartisan cosponsors in a resolution to designate July as Indian American Heritage Month." The Hindu American Foundation said it "was proud to support this bipartisan resolution.”

news.title: WNBA Finals stars risk more Trump fury as they walk off the court again for national anthem before Game 5
news.text:
The WNBA's Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries once again took a pass on the national anthem before Game 5 of the Finals on Monday in San Francisco.

Both teams took part in warmups before exiting the court at the Chase Center, only to reappear after Dinah Jane completed her rendition of The Star-Spangled Banner.

The WNBA suspended its mandatory anthem protocols in 2017 and currently allows teams to decide if they're going to be standing on the court while the song is played before games. For instance, the Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever do include the anthem as part of their pre-game routines, while the current finalists have opted against doing so.

Neither the Dream nor the Valkyries have claimed to be engaged in a political demonstration.

President Donald Trump commented on the situation at a political rally in Iowa last week. 

'By the way, what's going on with the Women's NBA? What's that all about?' Trump asked.

Trump then linked Dream and Valkyries players to former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who famously refused to stand for the anthem throughout the 2016 NFL season in protest of racist police brutality.

'No, it's a big deal going on,' Trump said. 'They leave the court when the national anthems play. What's that all about?

'You know, the NFL did that for a while and they stopped because people stopped watching the games. So I think you should do the same thing with women's basketball.'

Although its Nielsen ratings did decline somewhat, the NFL maintained the highest viewership of any American sports league before, during and after Kaepernick's 2016 demonstrations.

Trump is not the first Republican politician to weigh in on the WNBA anthem situation during the ongoing finals.

'I think it's disgraceful,' Vice President JD Vance told author Raymond Arroyo. 'I think that you should not express some criticism of a public policy of a given politician by disrespecting the country writ large.

'I mean, those women who play for the WNBA, think of the public safety, think of the incredible wealth and privilege, the amazing jobs that they have.

'They have a lot to be grateful to the United States for, and I think that if they had a bit more of a spirit of gratitude, they'd be happier people, and they wouldn't offend so many people as well.'

The Vice President added: 'Whether you were born in the United States or whether you came here by choice, this is your country. And I think that we're all meant to love it.

'We're all meant to try to make it the best version of itself. But fundamentally, I think, without love of country, I think that you're going to be a disordered human being.
news.summary: The WNBA's Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries once again took a pass on the national anthem before Game 5 of the Finals on Monday in San Francisco.

news.title: How a WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ became a force in Brazil election
news.text: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won Brazil’s presidential runoff, securing a fourth non-consecutive term after a closely contested election. However, the result faces a potential legal challenge from rival Flávio Bolsonaro, while US president Donald Trump has questioned the vote, alleging that it was “rigged”.Lula secured more than 64 million votes, defeating Bolsonaro, who received just under 60 million, by nearly 4.4 million votes. The incumbent is expected to take office on January 5, 2027, for a fourth non-consecutive term.A key factor in Lula’s comeback was the mobilisation of voters who had abstained in the first round or backed other candidates. An additional 14.1 million voters participated in the runoff, with analysts estimating that three-quarters of these votes went to Lula.Central to the campaign was lawmaker André Janones’ WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army”, which attracted nearly 11 million people and encouraged supporters to campaign on social media.Janones adopted an aggressive, sustained digital strategy, Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at Fundação Getulio Vargas in São Paulo told news agency AP.“He basically embraced the right’s style of aggressive politics, very intense, constant messaging,” Stuenkel said.“The defeat in the first round jolted the Lula campaign into action. The strategy during the first round was lacklustre and saw a lot of infighting,” he added, according to AP.Juliano Cortinhas, an international relations professor at the University of Brasília, said the digital campaign also helped pressure Meta, which owns WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook, over allegations of bias favouring Bolsonaro.“There was ‘external interference we were suffering by major platforms’,” Cortinhas told AP. He added: “It wasn't only Meta, many others were using their algorithms to repost many images and many messages of the far-right, and they did not do the same to the left.”Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on October 15 that Meta must ensure equal treatment of both candidates. The company subsequently said it had addressed the order.Meanwhile, Trump questioned the result on Monday, saying, “Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me.” He added: “I thought it had a very bad look, the way it was tabulated.”“It looked like another rigged election, frankly,” Trump said, without presenting evidence.Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to organise opposition to Lula and seek to nullify the results. He said, “I am going to gather elected lawmakers and senators to organize our strategy and make the lower house and the Senate our fortress against barbaric acts that are set to happen in another four years of Lula.”However, overturning the result would require evidence of fraud affecting Lula’s 4.4 million-vote margin and approval from Brazil’s eight-member electoral court before certification on December 18.Benjamin Gedan, director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, warned, “False claims of fraud are becoming commonplace, though that does not make them any less dangerous.”You use AI every day. Jay-Z has been tapped to headline the 2027 Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show.

The news was announced during halftime of the Cowboys vs. Eagles game during Monday Night Football. “It will be Jay-Z in SoFi on [Valentine’s Day],” ABC commentator Scott Van Pelt said. “We’ll all be looking forward to seeing that.”

“For several years, we’ve had the privilege of working closely with Jay-Z and Roc Nation, and I’ve seen the extraordinary impact he has had on the Super Bowl Halftime Show,” added NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell. “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him. “Jay-Z’s impact on global music culture is as profound as it is undeniable,” said Oliver Schusser, Apple’s vp of music and international content, in a statement. “We’ve had the privilege of working closely with him these last few years to bring some of the world’s most exciting and prolific artists to the Super Bowl Halftime Show stage and we are so thrilled that he will be taking that stage himself this year. We know it’s going to be an incredible show.”

Jay-Z joins a coveted list of artists who have earned the opportunity to headline the NFL’s biggest night, including his wife Beyoncé, Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Michael Jackson, Rihanna, Madonna, Lady Gaga, Bruce Springsteen, Diana Ross, Katy Perry, The Weeknd, Usher, The Rolling Stones and Bruno Mars, among many others.

The billionaire rap icon already curates the Halftime Show through his company Roc Nation in a deal with the NFL that began in 2019 and was renewed in 2024. Given his close connections with NFL powerbrokers, it was inevitable that Jay-Z would headline the marquee event at some point.

Super Bowl LXI will air on ABC and ESPN. The game will take place Sunday, Feb. 14, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, home of the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers.

Back in February, Bad Bunny brought his Latin love to the Super Bowl stage, turning Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California, into a big dance party. During his 13-minute set, he performed a wide range of his biggest hits, including “Tití Me Preguntó,” “Eoo,” “BAILE INoLVIDABLE,” “El Apagón,” “CAFé CON RON,” “MONACO,” NUEVAYoL” and “DtMF,” among others.

The Puerto Rican rapper and singer also told a love story throughout the performance, which included several celebrity cameos, and ended with a message of unity and love displayed on the screens inside the stadium, which read, “The only thing more powerful than hate is love.”

Jay-Z and the NFL first linked up in 2019, in a deal that saw the league and Roc Nation work together on events and social activism. The NFL would consult Roc Nation on its entertainment offerings, including the Super Bowl Halftime Show, and also work with the company “strengthen community through music and the NFL’s Inspire Change initiative.”

The league working with Jay-Z came in the wake of the NFL’s controversial treatment of former San Francisco 49ers player Colin Kaepernick, who was effectively forced out of the NFL for staging protests against police brutality and systemic racism. The legendary rapper initially publicly supported Kaepernick in his fight against the NFL.

But after Jay-Z was brought on board to essentially revitalize the league’s brand that had taken a battering over the Kaepernick affair, the two fell out. “[Jay-Z] has built the alignment with the NFL, the NFL that has blackballed me, the same NFL that, in a players-owners meeting in 2017, said we need a Black face to help us get rid of the protests,” Kaepernick told NBC News in September 2026.

news.title: D-Day for Netanyahu as Israel goes to the polls: 70,000 expat voters could kick out Bibi in election today
news.text:
Benjamin Netanyahu's political future hangs in the balance as Israel goes to the polls today in a defining vote for the Middle East.

The Israeli Prime Minister narrowly trails his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the country's first election since the October 7 massacre.

The deadliest day in Israel's history has featured prominently in the campaign - and the vote is widely seen as a referendum on the catastrophic security failure.

Voters heading to the polls will pass the faces of fallen soldiers peering from stickers on train station walls and faded yellow ribbons honouring the hostages, the last of whom were returned in a ceasefire deal last year.

Mr Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, has sought to shift blame for the failures surrounding October 7 to security officials, while touting Israel's military achievements against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and their patron, Iran.

Yesterday, Donald Trump doubled down on his support for Mr Netanyahu despite relations between the pair having been strained by the war on Iran.

The US President urged Israelis to vote for the Israeli PM so the pair could 'finish the job' in Iran.

In the Truth Social post, Mr Trump added: 'When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!'

He said: 'Israel was called the little satan, with the United States being called the big satan, by some very evil people.

'There can no longer be the chant heard around the world of 'Death to America, death to Israel,' and there won't be.'

Mr Netanyahu has made the confrontation with the regime in Tehran a key part of his campaign, pledging to work with Trump to eliminate the Iranian nuclear threat.

But former IDF chief Eisenkot has accused him of playing up the Iran threat when it suits him politically, and of failing to accomplish his war goals.

Mr Netanyahu's fate could be sealed by an estimated 70,000 Israeli expats who are flying back to the country to cast their vote, with many expected to back his opponent.

Among those who have returned is Hannah, a businesswoman from North West London who lived in Israel for 11 years and is determined to see a change of leadership.

Speaking to the Daily Mail, she said: 'This election is existential for the soul and future of Israel. I felt so strongly about its importance that I made a special trip back to Israel to cast my vote.

'I will be voting for Gadi Eisenkot because I believe our country desperately needs clear, strong and ethical leadership — leadership that can restore trust, bring people together and heal the divisions that Benjamin Netanyahu has failed to bridge.

'If Itamar Ben-Gvir and the extreme right continue to hold positions of power in the Israeli government, I fear Israel will become a country whose values no longer reflect those I believe in and identify with.'

Israelis abroad cannot generally vote by post, proxy or at their local embassy. With limited exceptions they must return to Israel in person to cast their ballots. The AID Coalition, a US-based non-profit, estimates that up to 67,000 Israelis are returning to vote, about half from the US and the rest from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

For many expatriates, the importance of this election outweighs the cost and inconvenience of returning home to vote.

The latest polling by Israeli broadcasters placed Mr Eisenkot's Yashar party a few seats ahead of Netanyahu's Likud.

But securing the largest number of seats would not, by itself, guarantee victory. The election is likely to be followed by complicated coalition negotiations, with any prospective government needing the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset.
news.summary: The Israeli Prime Minister narrowly trails his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the country's first election since the October 7 massacre.

news.title: Carney Says Trump Moving Closer to Canada's Trade Demands as Midterms Loom
news.text: Toronto: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that trade talks with US President Donald Trump's administration have picked up slightly, but any progress is because Washington is moving closer to Canada's demands. The comments come eight days before US midterm elections, with White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett suggesting the countries are close to a deal. “To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position,” Carney said. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc's office said Canada remains in “constructive dialogue” with Washington. Carney described a “slight, slight intensification” of discussions but said Canada's negotiating position remained unchanged. Asked how he could be sure US President Donald Trump would “sign in pen” this time, after Carney previously warned that Washington's signature was sometimes “written in pencil,” the prime minister replied, “I don't know that.” Canada rejected Washington's terms in August after the countries appeared close to a deal. Carney said the offer crossed Canadian “red lines.” Trump subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation and further trade restrictions. Trump said Friday he would lift some 50% tariffs on Canadian goods while imposing new tariffs on dozens of other products. Two days later, he told a Michigan campaign rally that Canada was “willing to give us anything at this moment” and that a deal would be settled “pretty soon.” He told a Detroit television station an agreement could come before the midterms, although it might take months. Trump's tariffs have become an issue in closely watched Senate races. Republican candidate Mike Rogers says in a Michigan campaign ad that Canada is “not our enemy” and “we need to end this tariff war now.” In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins pressed the Trump administration to ease tariffs on Canadian goods used by farmers and other businesses, with Washington announcing exemptions Friday. Trump has repeatedly complained about the US trade deficit with Canada, but energy more than accounts for the gap. The United States buys millions of barrels of Canadian oil daily, typically at a discount, and runs a trade surplus with Canada when energy is excluded. Trump also wants automakers to move production from Canada to the United States, threatening an industry deeply integrated across the border for decades. Trump's trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st US state have pushed Carney to seek new markets, with a goal of doubling Canadian exports outside the United States over the next decade. Carney hosts European Union leaders Thursday and Friday in Montreal to pursue closer economic and security ties. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the EU's first associate member, a status that has yet to be defined.

news.title: Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges
news.text: President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz that has highlighted Republicans' challenges ahead of an election that could drastically shift power in Washington and statehouses across the country.“I'm here because Cindy’s doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can’t take a chance,” Trump told the crowd, his voice audibly hoarse, as he worked to boost Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is facing a surprisingly stiff challenge from Democrat Scott Colom.Colom was spotted at the rally site, too, creating the rare spectacle of Trump's staunchest supporters interacting directly with a figure the president would soon go on to denigrate as a “Marxist radical” and “fake" and “shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate” from the stage.Mississippi, among the nation’s most reliably Republican states, is not where the GOP envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Colom is one of many Democratic underdogs who have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps because of widespread voter discontent over inflation, the Iran war and other aspects of Trump’s second presidency.He said he had planned to go to the rally site to listen to what was on Trump supporters' minds."They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said ahead of the president's arrival.Trump's event kicks off a week of aggressive campaigning that will include more stops in states he won comfortably in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Iowa.RELATED STORY | Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to goDemocrats, including progressives, are expanding their effortsTop Democratic candidates and their surrogates were also greeting voters — more than 30 million of whom have already cast ballots, according to data collected by The Associated Press from election administrators across the country — as they try to end Republicans' threadbare majority in the House, take over a Senate majority that was once thought secure for Republicans and end the GOP’s national advantage in state capitals.Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' 2024 presidential candidate, campaigned in Wisconsin with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who faces Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, for governor. Crowley would be the state’s first Black governor if elected to lead the battleground state.“This is a tight race because the stakes are so high,” Harris said at the event billed as a “Women for Crowley” rally.Meanwhile, in Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from an ad created by a political action committee called Rebellion PAC that blames high grocery prices on U.S. support for Israel.“This ad is not affiliated in any way with the Abdul for Senate campaign,” a spokesperson for El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, said in a statement about the spot, which features a couple discussing U.S. support for Israel as they shop for groceries.“Apparently it’s costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza,” the woman says.The ad had been condemned by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic primary.The way to win Michigan “is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world,” Stevens wrote on X.El-Sayed, who would be the country’s first Muslim senator, has denounced antisemitism while fiercely criticizing Israel for its military operations in Gaza — a position that has been a frequent point of attack for both Republicans and supporters of Israel in his party.Vance campaigning in other Republican statesVice President JD Vance traveled to Kansas to stump for Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight contest with Democratic nominee and pastor Adam Hamilton. Hundreds of people were gathered inside the warehouse of a steel-fabricating company in north Topeka in a state where Democrats haven’t won a Senate race since 1932.Marshall told the crowd that Trump is on the ballot, even if his name doesn’t appear, because of how Democrats will thwart his agenda if they win control of Congress.“Democrats are coming out like it’s a presidential year,” he said, calling on the GOP to match Democrats’ energy.Jace Sullivan, a 50-year-old electrician from Topeka who describes himself as “85% Republican,” said Trump supporters need to “circle the wagons” and get out to vote.Wearing a red “JD Vance for President 2028" shirt, he said he thinks Trump is rightly working to keep Iran from getting nuclear weapons.“Gas prices are high and it does suck, but it’s a means to an end,” Sullivan said.Trump, at the Mississippi rally, said he had, in fact, expected gas prices to rise even higher than they had.“It worked out fine and it’ll be over soon,” he said of the war with Iran.Earlier, Vance was in Belgrade, Montana, to campaign with Republican Aaron Flint, who is facing Democrat Sam Forstag in the race for the state’s 1st Congressional District, and Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme.Sen. Tim Scott, who serves as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told The Associated Press Monday that GOP candidates are “closing very strongly” in races across the country, including South Carolina, which Trump is set to visit for the second time in as many weeks to stump for GOP Sen. Darline Graham.“One of the reasons why we will be in the majority is because he has invested the time and the energy on the campaign trail,” Scott said on the sidelines of U.S. Rep. Russell Fry’s 3rd Annual Freedom Fry event.RELATED STORY | Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel ‘far closer than it should’Trump to rally in another reliably Republican stateBut it's Trump's visit to Mississippi that perhaps brings the midterm landscape into the sharpest relief with just a week of campaigning left.To be sure, Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points.But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history as Mississippi's first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump's lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith's mistakes into an upset.Senate Democrats’ super PAC has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2 million investment. Mississippians have not chosen a new Democratic senator since 1947, and Democrats last won a Senate race there when that senator, the onetime segregationist John Stennis, won his last reelection in 1982.In New York, meanwhile, one of the party’s most vulnerable House members pulled from Trump’s campaign playbook. Rep. Mike Lawler, who is in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley in New York City’s northern suburbs, manned a McDonald’s drive-thru — mimicking something Trump did two years ago, even as Lawler has tried to emphasize his independence from the president.
news.summary: President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz.
news.author: AP via Scripps News Group

news.title: Trump warns of '1929 style economic depression' if Democrats win Congress
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 27 (IANS) President Donald Trump warned that a Democratic victory in next week's congressional elections could plunge the United States into an economic depression, as he sought to rally Republican voters with promises of cash payments, lower taxes, tougher immigration laws and an early end to the war with Iran. Addressing a campaign rally in Mississippi, Trump portrayed the November 3 midterm elections as a decisive test of his presidency. The President offered a sweeping defence of his administration's record, claiming unprecedented investment commitments, declining crime, expanding manufacturing and American military dominance over Iran. He also renewed criticism of Canada's trade policies and pledged to give every adult American citizen $5,000 if Republicans retained both chambers of Congress. "If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929 style economic depression," Trump told supporters gathered at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth. The rally was organised to support Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, who faces Democratic challenger Scott Colom in the November 3 election. Trump promised a cash payment to American adults if Republicans won both the House of Representatives and Senate. "If Republicans win the House of Representatives and Senate, I am going to give all adult citizens in the United States $5,000," he said. Trump claimed that tariff revenues and economic growth would provide sufficient resources to finance the programme. He estimated its cost at approximately $1 trillion and insisted that the federal government could afford the expenditure. "The only caveat is you have to spend the money in the United States of America," he said. The President did not explain how the proposed payments would be distributed, whether congressional approval would be required or how the domestic spending restriction would be enforced. The announcement was a campaign promise rather than an approved federal payment programme. Trump devoted a substantial portion of his address to the conflict with Iran, defending American military operations and predicting that hostilities would end soon. He claimed that US forces had severely damaged Iran's naval, air and nuclear capabilities and established an effective maritime blockade. The President said Iran had been close to developing a nuclear weapon before American military intervention. He claimed that 159 Iranian naval vessels had been destroyed and that hundreds of Iranian fighter aircraft had been rendered inoperable. Trump also said the United States had established control over maritime traffic involving Iran, including the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. He asserted that oil shipments through the waterway had recovered despite the conflict. The President acknowledged that he had anticipated a substantial increase in global oil prices following military operations but said the situation had developed more favourably than expected. He predicted that energy prices would decline further when the conflict ended. Trump also criticised earlier American administrations for failing to confront Iran's nuclear ambitions more aggressively. Defending his economic policies, Trump claimed that tariffs had encouraged foreign manufacturers to establish production facilities in the United States. He said his administration had secured investment commitments worth $22.2 trillion, describing the figure as unprecedented. Trump also turned his attention to Canada, accusing the neighbouring country of maintaining unfair trade barriers against American agricultural products. He claimed that Ottawa was eager to reach a new agreement with Washington. "Canada's treated us badly, but they want to make a deal badly, so we'll get that taken care of," Trump said. The President specifically criticised Canadian dairy tariffs, citing rates of 400 per cent. Trump also repeated his assertion that he had renamed a lake bordering Canada as Lake America. Trump pledged that a Republican-controlled Congress would pursue additional restrictions on illegal immigration and strengthen election identification requirements. He said his administration would seek legislation preventing future presidents from reopening the country's borders to unauthorised migrants. The President also promised to pursue restrictions on sanctuary cities and tougher penalties for major drug traffickers, human traffickers and those convicted of killing police officers. "We will pass the voter Identification Proof of Citizenship and Save America Act to defend our American elections from theft and fraud," he said. He also promised further legislative action on transgender participation in women's sports and gender-related medical procedures involving children. news.title: ‘The View’ Addresses Rumors About Firing Trump Nemesis
news.text:
The View has set the record straight on the fate of Joy Behar.

A rep for the daytime talk show confirmed to Entertainment Weekly that the veteran co-host, 84, won’t be leaving the program anytime soon, despite a report from RadarOnline.com last week saying otherwise.

The rep told EW that “there is no truth” to the report alleging Behar was on the outs amid a rumored “panel shake-up” because of “producers looking to make the show less shrill and more inviting to a broader audience.”

The report said concerns arose about Behar’s place on the program after she missed several weeks on the air due to an injury.

Behar, who joined the program as an original co-host alongside Barbara Walters in 1997, suffered a shoulder dislocation late last month, sidelining her from the talk show throughout October.

Her co-host Sunny Hostin addressed Behar’s absence on Oct. 1, saying that “she’s recovering and will be back soon.”

The View producer Brian Teta shared Monday that Behar’s return was imminent, announcing on Monday’s episode of the Behind the Table podcast that she will appear on the show for the first time since Sept. 30 on Tuesday.

“Joy is back,” Teta said at the end of the episode. “We’ve missed her. We’ll see you tomorrow!”

The Daily Beast has reached out to ABC News for comment.

Behar’s co-hosts have been keen to welcome the comedian back to the table.

“We’ll have something special when you know you’re on your way back. Hurry back,” Whoopi Goldberg said last week. “It’s not the same at the table. We miss you, we do.”

Goldberg had previously shared a message from Behar during her birthday episode on Oct. 7, which she missed because of her injury.

“She says, ‘Thanks to everyone who inquired about my recovery. If I was still 21, I’d have bounced back the next day,’” Goldberg said at the time. “‘But, since I’m an old bat, recuperating takes a bit longer. I plan to be back next week to fill everyone in on all the gory details.’”

It’s not the first time an injury has kept Behar away from the table.

Last year, after vanishing from the program for a few days, she informed viewers that she had broken her toe after “dropping an iPad” on her foot.

Behar, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump, told New York Magazine earlier this month that she would love to welcome him back to the View table.

“I’d love Donald Trump to take the heat. You can’t go to Fox all the time,” she said about the president, who had appeared on the program 18 times before his first presidency.

news.title: QUENTIN LETTS: His policies are as skimpy as his shorts, but after 100 days of watching Andy Burnham up close, this is what I've learned about our Daytime TV Prime Minister
news.text:
When a batsman reaches a century, cricket spectators stand and applaud. As Andy Burnham today reaches his 100th day as Prime Minister, few may feel the urge to leap up and honour that custom.

The only things rising are questions and doubts and debt levels. And, weirdly, Labour’s previously horizontal poll ratings. Was it really only 100 days ago that unhappy donkey Sir Keir Starmer was led to the glue factory?

If the nasal knight already seems ancient history, so do his cronies: Lord Hermer, the squeaky international-law obsessive who was Sir Keir’s Attorney General; Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor Who Cried; David Lammy, the Mastermind contestant who thought Henry VIII was succeeded by Henry VII.

How we miss them.

In sauntered Eyelashes Andy, the Manchester mayor with a touch of daytime TV. His adoring mum was in the crowd in Downing Street to greet him. His equally adoring wife Frankie gave up her marketing directorship at an electric-car-charging company to concentrate on supporting her spouse. She was going to be the new Jackie Kennedy.

Mr Burnham, once a Cabinet minister under Gordon Brown, had been out of national politics so long that he felt new. The muddy accent, the brushed-forward Caesar hairdo, the black leisure wear: he was different from Starmer and not as awkward, although possibly less intellectual.

The ministers around him were not up to much.

Right-hand woman Louise Haigh radiated a pub-moll’s menace, not least towards her dimwit colleague Lucy Powell. Linda and Janine in EastEnders have nothing on these two.

And for all the talk about Mr Burnham being trustworthy, it was rum the way he entrusted the Treasury to John Healey, whose resignation as Defence Secretary had helped topple Starmer. Had Burnham and Healey been in cahoots all along?

And jeepers, why did he appoint that snaggle-toothed maniac Ed Miliband to be Foreign Secretary? Some said getting Red Ed out of the energy department would allow Labour to drop Net Zero. Yet the new Secretary of State, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has proved almost as much of an eco-zealot.

Red Ed, meanwhile, has been causing diplomatic chaos, shaking hands with an apparatchik from the murderous Iranian regime and imposing sanctions on Israel’s West Bank.

The Netanyahu government retaliated by supporting Argentina’s claims to the Falklands.

Another Miliband triumph.

After winning June 18’s Makerfield by-election – on a promise not to reopen Brexit squabbles – Mr Burnham blithely said it was time for everything to change. Most immediately that meant a new pair of running shorts. The old ones had shown too much inner (hairy) thigh.

He also took the thrusting decision to open a new branch office of Whitehall in Manchester. This was to be called ‘No10 North’ and it had a splashy opening at which the country’s top civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo, pawed at Mr Burnham like a hungry spaniel.

Since then ‘No10 North’ has largely disappeared from the news. Its chief contribution to the economy so far has been to generate hefty bills in the form of rail fares to Manchester for London-based officials.

With Parliament going into recess as soon as he was in office, the new PM had a long and breezy summer. Two weeks into the new job, off he tottered on a foreign holiday.

We were told that he would spend August on a ‘nationwide listening tour’. There were photographs of him in Sheffield putting a carton of oat milk into a shopping bag marked ‘Feeling Jammy’. After that, the ‘I’m Not Listening Tour’ rather fizzled out.

The new man’s policy positions were as skimpy as his running shorts. In his first speech outside No10 (the one in London) he said he would end rough-sleeping.

Having walked through central London, Liverpool, Brighton and Birmingham at night in recent weeks, I’d say there is little sign of that.

Mr Burnham has boasted of lowering living costs. Prices have in fact risen since June. He wants to build more homes. The housing market has bombed. He has promised re-industrialisation. In recent days a major AI data centre planned for Loughton, Essex, has been scrapped owing to grid delays.

How does he respond to these pratfalls? Ignores them! Sails onwards, fluttering his eyelashes. And it seems to be working. Opinion polls suggest a Labour bounce of several points since Sir Keir was turned into a tube of Uhu.

Polls hypnotise politicians but how accurate a guide are they to election results? Theresa May went into the 2017 general election some 20 points ahead and blew that lead. In general election campaigns, policies may matter more than eyelashes.

What, if anything, does Andy Burnham actually think? Exactly how does he intend to get tramps off the streets, minimise planning delays, incentivise manufacturers and cut household costs?

No one knows, perhaps not even he.

Aides have briefed this and that but details are always elusive. After the past 100 days we know no more about his costed proposals than we did when he sashayed into the Commons on June 22 to take the oath as the new MP for Makerfield.

Maybe that will change tomorrow with the Budget. Don’t count on it. Labour MPs have little appetite for cutting our ruinous welfare spending.

One of Burnham’s former economics advisers, Andy Haldane, has said that unless welfare is reduced we could have a re-run of the Liz Truss mini-Budget. The need for action is intense.

Will urgent decisions follow? Or will we instead be told there is going to be ‘a conversation’?

On one of his first prime ministerial engagements Mr Burnham visited a care home in north London where we were told his Government would hold ‘a big conversation about national care’.

The PM did say in his conference speech – the one in which he cried about his late father – that he would break the triple-lock on pensions. Mind you, that will not happen until April 2030 at the earliest. Urgency would appear to be lacking.

Two days ago, Mr Burnham, having broken his by-election promise and reopened the Brexit question, said he wanted ‘an honest conversation’ about our returning to free movement with the European Union. When a politician speaks of his ‘honesty’, count the spoons.

As for ‘conversations’, they are easier than rigorous prime ministerial despatch.

As a parliamentary performer so far he has been unstirring. From my Commons gallery perch I can see behind the Speaker’s chair. When Mr Burnham enters, milling MPs do not recoil or tingle as they have done with earlier PMs.

He looks at the floor as he walks. He does not bother much with his briefing notes. Nor does he weigh his words obviously before spooning out responses.

It is as if he is unfazed by his high office, little fussed. One of life’s amblers.

Domestically in the last 100 days, little has been done. Globally the same period has seen extraordinary upheavals. Donald Trump’s presidency has spiralled towards likely mid-term election defeats.

The US President has done a smelly diesel deal with Moscow while his ally Elon Musk, or someone close to him, fiddled about with the Starlink satellites and made it harder for Ukraine to defend herself against Russia’s bombardment of Ukrainian civilians.

The White House also called for Kiev’s President Zelensky to be toppled. The doughty, diminutive Zelensky is three times as big a man as Trump or Vladimir Putin but no one in the Burnham Government had the guts to say so.

With the Middle East unstable; oil and gas prices have gone haywire, diesel reaching £2 a litre in Britain, with inevitable consequences for inflation. Argentina, encouraged by Benjamin Netanyahu and an unhinged Trump, has threatened the Falklands.

Moscow has rattled its warheads and snooped on our sea-bed cables.

And Europe has burst into flames twice. When summer fires broke out across the Continent our environmentally-pure Government tutted. Then came violent protests in France, Germany, Italy, Portugal and Albania, with city centres smashed and torched. The unrest triggered racism and vigilante fightbacks. Andy Burnham said almost nothing. A shrew makes more noise.

When he did have a chance to appear alongside Mr Trump, it did not go well.

The two met briefly at the United Nations in September. Mr Burnham clutched his legs, cast beseeching looks to Ed Miliband and generally looked tiny. In foreign policy, the blokeish Mancunian thing doesn’t work. Rival statesmen just scent weakness.

Brussels, listening to Mr Burnham’s prostrate, ill-thought-through come-hithers, must think once-proud Britain has surrendered. Labour supporters don’t mind this. They never liked British sovereign power. Voters may be more discerning.

Why, therefore, do current polls seem to favour this shallow scrutiny-dodger?

Well, those eyelashes have been putting themselves about on social media. Mr Burnham has done numerous TikTok videos. He has met – roll the drums, please – teenage influencers and been on something called Gogglebox.

He has talked about pork scratchings and Twiglets and football (although he becomes batey if asked about Manchester City and its financial scandal).

He made a video with ‘Bus Aunty’, a woman who is keen on double-decker buses. Mr Burnham is himself a fan of buses, although nowadays he must rough it in the back of an armour-plated Range Rover.

He even did podcasts with the football commentator Gary Lineker and with Alastair Campbell. More rigorous interviewers were not granted such access.

He has also proved good at slogans. His conference tagline was ‘hope again’, tacit recognition that Labour under Sir Keir became embogged in glumness. Hope is never a bad thing for a politician to embrace.

With the Greens in disarray, Marxist types may be drifting back to Labour now that Mr Burnham has wrenched it Leftwards on Israel and the EU. Labour MPs are happier.

The same cannot be said of a country which has never been taxed more. Youth unemployment has soared above European rates thanks to Labour’s tax hikes on employers. Domestic fuel prices are hellishly high, in part thanks to Net Zero.

Business confidence has dropped like a dead snipe. And with Parliament having resumed, Mr Burnham is finding it harder to dodge questions.

When Kemi Badenoch harpoons him he wails about his desire for ‘problem-solving not point-scoring’. What happens if the problems, such as employment and energy costs, are being caused by his party’s policies?

Perhaps we will learn more tomorrow. Not that Mr Burnham will be to the fore. Budget Day belongs to a Chancellor.

The PM is just a front bench adornment, two set of eyelashes sitting mute; as silent, again, as a Royal Navy submarine under the polar icecap.

Down periscope, dive, dive, dive. That’s how it was for the first 100 days. For all the talk, little is likely to change.
news.summary: Was it really only 100 days ago that unhappy donkey Sir Keir Starmer was led to the glue factory? In sauntered Eyelashes Andy, the mayor with a touch of daytime TV
news.author: Editor,Quentin Letts

news.title: Brent Crude Falls Below $115/Barrel After Saudi Initiates De-Escalation Talks With Iran
news.text: Crude oil prices extended their decline for another session on Tuesday after diplomacy efforts between Saudi Arabia and Tehran picked up, but still traded near $115 per barrel levels. Global benchmark Brent Crude was down 0.73% to $114.94 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate traded 0.72% lower at $101.05 per barrel. The slight relief came as Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman held a meeting with with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran on Monday. The talks were held after repeated attacks by Yemen-based and Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.Additionally, senior officials from Pakistan and Turkey also joined the de-escalation discussions in Tehran. Separately, Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to with his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, as well as Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, on the sidelines of an energy summit in Moscow on Tuesday. Despite negotiation efforts, risks to energy supply linger prominently and shipping costs remain elevated. US President Donald Trump said that he expected the price of oil to go "much much higher", adding that he was "fully prepared" to do it as they "really had no choice."Addressing the Iran war in an election rally in Mississippi, Trump stated that he never really liked the temporary ceasefire between the warring blocs. Elsewhere, Hezbollah is preparing for a new regional war in Lebanon after receiving funds from Iran, Reuters reported. The Saudi-led coalition said that it destroyed three drones in Riyadh, which followed clashes involving Tehran-backed Houthi rebels.Brent has suged about 90% this year as the war disrupted energy supplies and expanded to involve Yemen's Houthi rebels. The risk of further attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping routes remains a concern for markets, even as crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near prewar levels.ALSO READ: Oil Shock Loading? Analysts Aren't Ruling Out Brent At $200 Because Of These FactorsThe $200 Per Barrel Threat The market broadly agrees that the worst-case scenario for commodities, feared at the start of the US-Iran war in March this year, has failed to materialise. The worst that the oil market witnessed was in April-end, when Brent futures had climbed to as high as $126 a barrel. Despite the conflict still underway—with both sides appearing on the edge of escalating their military offensives—crude has met a stiff resistance at $110. That extreme scenario of oil hitting $200, that faded over the summer, is now back in the conversation. The world's biggest independent oil trader says only a makeshift shipping arrangement is keeping it at bay. Meanwhile, crude stocks in the Middle East and the West are near their limits.
news.summary: Despite negotiation efforts, risks to energy supply linger prominently and shipping costs remain elevated.
news.author: Khushi Maheshwari

news.title: Architect struck off after calling neighbour racist for cheering on England is 'malicious and vindictive' and 'made things up', victims say
news.text:
An architect banned from working for two years after calling her neighbour a racist for supporting England is 'malicious and vindictive', according to one of her victims. 

Dr Karin Elliott's allegations were branded 'ridiculous' by a neighbour who was accused of 'gender-based violence' because of the way he drove his vehicle.

Retired tree surgeon Steve Davis was accused of making a deliberately 'phallic' gesture by leaving his white Nissan Navara truck on the driveway he shared with Dr Elliott in Norwich.

Along with accusing another neighbour of racism for cheering on England's sports teams, Dr Elliott also claimed that a neighbour's garden wall was a politically motivated stunt in a campaign of abuse between December 2023 and early 2024. 

Elliott's false claims saw her barred from working as an architect when the Architects Registration Board ruled they amounted to misconduct. 

Responding to their recent decision, Mr Davis told the Daily Mail: 'This is not even a neighbours' dispute, it is an architect carrying on some sort of personal vendetta for reasons known only to herself and her partner.

'Her false allegations just were not true. I think she was vindictive and malicious. Her suggestion that my vehicle was phallic was ridiculous.

'The story is about three sets of neighbours being falsely and publicly accused by Ms Elliott of racism, sexual and physical harassment and violence, theft, malicious damage and abuse of power. None of these accusations were true.' 

Dr Elliott, who prided herself on her American-Irish ancestry, along with her French lover Francois Girardin, alleged a neighbour's garden wall was built to coincide with American President Donald Trump erecting a wall to keep immigrants out of the US.

Mr Girardin also complained that whenever England played sport, a neighbour would 'leave their doors open, and – especially when England played France – their family would cheer for England'.

Mr Davis added: 'We had a skip on our land during building work on our house which meant I could not use our normal parking spaces.

'I thought it would be OK to park in the shared area for that period as she had done so herself. Her suggestion that my vehicle was phallic was ridiculous.'

At the tribunal during cross-examination, Ms Elliott said from 'a psychoanalytic perspective' her neighbour's car could be seen as a 'phallic symbol' and a manifestation of gender violence. 

The tribunal found this 'underscored how tenuously she constructed serious accusations against other people, and how casually she dispensed them'.

The architect had made a planning application for the installation of CCTV cameras on her property in December 2023 following disputes with her neighbours.

She wrote a letter to local residents in February 2024 asking for support for her application and made serious allegations about her neighbours that the tribunal considered to be 'dishonest' and 'misleading'.

In the letter to residents, she claimed one neighbour had 'smashed down several of our historic walls, chopped down many of our historic trees, and built on our property, all without our consent'.

Discussing another neighbour, Ms Elliott wrote: 'He calls us either a "piece of s***", "disgusting" and/or exclaims "the stench" regularly.'

In another allegation, the architect wrote: 'He threatened to hit one of us over the head with a hammer at one stage, after he was asked to desist.

'He had been starting to build a wall on our property illegally on a Sunday, following Trump's declaration that he would "Build a big wall" to keep out immigrants.

'It is very upsetting. We are Irish/American and French.'

Mr Davis said he and two other neighbours had given evidence at the tribunal which held four weeks of hearings over 14 months before coming to its conclusion. 

The tribunal found Ms Elliott's conduct occurred after she had previously been found guilty of unacceptable professional conduct in 2021 for calling neighbours 'racists and Nazis' as well as 'making offensive references to their physical characteristics and mental health'. 

Mr Davis added: 'We thought that after the gas chamber and Nazi stuff, things would die down, but they didn't.'

Another neighbour who was only identified as C at the tribunal hearing said he was pleased the ordeal was over. 

He said: 'We welcome with relief the outcome of the independent ARB investigation in the unprofessional conduct of Ms Elliott. 

'The ARB pointed to an ongoing "vendetta" by Ms Elliott and we would point anyone to read the findings to fully understand what we have all endured. 

'We hope this outcome will make her stop these libellous accusations and allow us to move on.'

 Dr Elliott refused to comment last night at her Gothic-style home when she was approached.
news.summary: Dr Karin Elliott's allegations were branded 'ridiculous' by a neighbour who was accused of gender-based violence because of the way he drove his vehicle.
news.author: Cameron Charters,Editor

news.title: Russian forces introduce ceasefire in Kherson direction
news.text:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces introduced a ceasefire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) to prepare for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.

"As part of preparations for a humanitarian operation near the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, the Russian Armed Forces ceased fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27," the statement reads.

Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov announced on October 23 that the Russian Armed Forces would cease fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 to allow for a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki.

According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the Kiev regime has been shelling roads leading to Alyoshki and extensively using drones to destroy vehicles. Ukrainian forces have also been using unmanned aerial vehicles to lay mines along roads to prevent civilian evacuations and impede the delivery of foods, medicine and other essential supplies to Alyoshki.

Over the past week alone, the Kiev regime carried out 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone strikes on Alyoshki and main roads in the area, while Russian troops devised over 300 landmines and other explosive devices.

On September 21, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the situation in Alyoshki as critical, saying that food and medicine could not be delivered there amid ongoing Ukrainian shelling and drone attacks. Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9. Putin said the parties had agreed that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova would remain in constant contact with US First Lady Melania Trump's office.

Peskov pointed out on October 26 that the agreement to conduct a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki could set a precedent for similar missions in other areas. He particularly highlighted the United States’ direct and constructive role in coordinating the process. Peskov added that Russia hoped Ukraine would honor all agreements concerning the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
news.summary: The ceasefire is part of the preparations for a humanitarian operation near the town of Alyoshki

news.title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director’s lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.

The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration’s targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections.

“Well, they’re back — again,” Comey said in a video statement Monday. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary.”

The Justice Department said it had filed what’s known as a “criminal information” to extend the statute of limitations for when they can permissibly bring an indictment.

“Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” a department spokesperson said.

An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury’s finding of probable cause to a court. Comey’s lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by a 10-year statute of limitations.

“For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence,” his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.

The allegation was previously investigated

The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.

Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI’s conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a recent court filing.

In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name “Tropical Vortex.” But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.

“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an “Information” against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said.

Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey “sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before” that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns “and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”

The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 6, 2016, 10 years after the story was published. “But,” Comey’s lawyers said, “the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice.”

They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.

Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history

The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case he has sought to dismiss and some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

The cases are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey’s daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration.

But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president — an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey’s firing. Comey in 2018 published a memoir, “A Higher Loyalty,” that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him “untethered to truth.” Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for “treason” — an accusation Comey dismissed as “dumb lies” — and called him an “untruthful slime ball.”

news.title: Netanyahu’s political survival on the line as Israel votes
news.text:
JERUSALEM — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel’s election on Tuesday, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks, wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel’s deepening international isolation.

Yet Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel’s fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.

Opinion polls show a close race between Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the center.

Mr. Netanyahu is campaigning on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran. Mr. Netanyahu said on Sunday that Mr. Trump was prepared to act again to “finally” remove the Iranian threat, but only if Mr. Netanyahu remained in power.

Mr. Eisenkot has accused Mr. Netanyahu of “relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats,” and said he was confident Mr. Trump would work “in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people.”

Mr. Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to form a government. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Mr. Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party has gained support in opinion polls.

Neither Mr. Netanyahu nor Mr. Eisenkot has a clear path to power. If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Mr. Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held next year.

Polls open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. (0500 to 2000 GMT).

THE OCTOBER 7 RECKONING
The election follows one of Israel’s most turbulent periods since its establishment in 1948, shaped by the trauma of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Israel’s subsequent military assault in Gaza and deep domestic divisions over the policies of Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government.

For many of Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of October 7, Israel’s deadliest day.

Mali Hajaj, an Education Ministry employee and Eisenkot supporter, said “the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that’s where our healing will come from.”

Lisa Tortor said she hoped Mr. Netanyahu would go and “they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel’s image.” Bibi is Mr. Netanyahu’s nickname.

But Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, rejected the idea Mr. Netanyahu was to blame for October 7 and called him “the right man for the state of Israel.”

“Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way,” Ms. Gabay said.

THE WARTIME RECORD
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after October 7, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks killed 74,000 people.

Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year’s joint US-Israeli war.

Mr. Eisenkot has said Israel’s next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by force or through an “arrangement” such as a US-backed diplomatic solution.

THE COALITION MATH
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Mr. Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.

But he has criticized Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states, and opposes Mr. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Mr. Ben-Gvir and Mr. Smotrich.

In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Mr. Netanyahu. Some have turned away from Mr. Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.

A high turnout among voters from Israel’s Arab minority, Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage, could help nudge Israel’s complex coalition arithmetic in favor of Mr. Eisenkot.

Though Mr. Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they prop up a minority government he leads in order to ensure Mr. Netanyahu is removed from office.

“My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide,” said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute. — Reuters

news.title: Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
news.text:
WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump’s public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week’s record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

Mr. Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.

The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a “generic ballot” question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.

That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.

For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Mr. Trump’s agenda in the last two years ​of his second term as president.

Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not ‌capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.

STEEP SENATE CLIMB FOR DEMOCRATS
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.

It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%.

The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Mr. Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.

Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.

The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters. — Reuters

news.title: Trump offers $1 million for reporting voter fraud in midterms
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has offered Americans a reward of $1 million if they report voter fraud in the 2026 midterm elections.

To qualify for the payment Trump has offered, he said in his Truth Social post on Monday the report must lead to the arrest and conviction of the suspected fraudster, reports The US Sun.

The offer follows the $5,000 ‘Trump dividend’ he promised at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas on 9 September if the Senate and the House remain in Republican control after November 3.

Trump has repeatedly claimed voter fraud, however there is no evidence of this in US elections at this scale.

The post does not provide details on the timescale of payments or how they would be funded.

“So if Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told attendees.

“It will be called the Trump dividend.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson told NBC’s Meet the Press in response to Trump’s proposal: “I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that, like I have to do everything else.”

“I never go out and give big commitments on the front end because I’ve got to work through it, and that’s what we do every single day.

“I’ll work with the president hand-in-hand, as I do all the time, and we’ll deliver for the American people. That’s the promise.”

Democrats were quick to take aim at the $5,000 proposal, which could cost $1.3 trillion, according to the US Sun, and has not been approved by Congress.

Many Democratic lawmakers have said Trump’s attempts to incentivise voters through cash payments are an attempt to stop the expected election day blue wave on Capitol Hill.

Senator Alex Padilla and Representative Robert Garcia said Trump was using taxpayer money as ‘slush funds’ to ‘buy votes’, according to the report.

In the past Trump has refused to acknowledge his 2020 defeat by former President Joe Biden and cited the expansion of voting by mail during Covid-19.

Trump’s former Attorney General, William Barr, denied evidence of voter fraud had been found.

“To date, we have not seen fraud on a scale that could have affected a different outcome in the election,” Barr told the Associated Press in December 2020.

“There’s been one assertion that would be systemic fraud, and that would be the claim that machines were programmed essentially to skew the election results.

“And the D.H.S. and D.O.J. have looked into that, and so far, we haven’t seen anything to substantiate that.”

news.title: Carney Says US Is ‘Coming Closer to Our Position’ on Trade Talks
news.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Washington has moved closer to Ottawa’s position in trade negotiations. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, repeated over the weekend his position that Canada is taking advantage of the United States, and that the matter will be “settled pretty soon.”

“To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” Carney said at a press conference in Ottawa on Oct. 26.The prime minister reiterated that his government is prepared to sign a trade agreement in Canada’s interest, but had set “very clear” red lines that prevented it from agreeing to a deal in August.

“To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there’s a greater prospect of a deal,” he said.Days earlier, at a press conference in Istanbul, Turkey, Carney said his government was prepared to wait months or even until “another administration” takes power in the United States before it signs a deal.

Trump had said at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25 that the trade negotiations would be settled “pretty soon” and that Canada was “willing to give us anything at this moment.” He added that Canada had been “ripping off” the United States for many years.Trade negotiations broke down in August, with Carney saying Washington had made unacceptable demands involving restrictions on Canada’s ability to pursue trade agreements with other countries, the exclusion of medium- and heavy-duty trucks from tariff exemptions, and weaker protections for the French language and Canadian culture. Trump administration officials have accused Ottawa of raising additional demands at the last moment.

The White House imposed 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods on Aug. 22, the day after Carney walked away from trade negotiations. Canada followed suit on Sept. 8, imposing retaliatory tariffs of 15, 25, and 50 percent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports.Washington imposed import bans on most Canadian alcoholic beverages, some dairy-related products, and motorcycles, beginning Sept. 29. The United States has also threatened to raise tariffs on automotive and steel products from 25 percent to 50 percent beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, in response to Ottawa’s counter-tariffs.Chief Canadian trade negotiator Janice Charette said on Oct. 22 that there is no timeline for resuming formal trade talks with the United States. She said she believed Washington would not fully remove tariffs on Canadian goods because of the revenue they generate for the U.S. government.
