news.title: Trump rants at Obama for comparing president’s White House decor to a Cheesecake Factory
news.text:
Donald Trump lashed out at Barack Obama during his Mississippi rally after the former Democratic president insulted his White House decor, comparing it to a Cheesecake Factory.

“He said, 'This isn't a Cheesecake Factory.' Can you believe it?” Trump told the crowd Monday night, apparently still irked by Obama’s dig from the weekend. “Which is a very successful company," Trump continued. “He doesn't like successful companies.”

Commentators noted on social media that Trump was “BIG MAD” after Obama ridiculed the additions to the White House — including gold accents, a ballroom and a South Lawn helicopter pad. 

“Guy’s building a ballroom that’s bigger than the White House,” Obama said Saturday at an Ohio rally. “He’s paved over the Rose Garden. Put a helicopter pad on the South Lawn, and there’s gold everywhere. What’s up with the gold? Everything, more gold!”

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory!” Obama quipped.

It was the second time the president raged against Obama’s joke on Monday.

“I’ve taken care of the White House,” Trump said earlier en route to the rally. “I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world. We reskinned it. It was in horrible shape.”

“For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory...that just shows why you were a lousy president,” he said.

Journalist Aaron Rupar posted a clip of Trump’s remarks to his 1.1 million followers. “Trump is BIG MAD about Obama saying the White House now looks like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory,” he said.

“Obama definitely hit a nerve,” a user replied.

“Uh oh. Somebody got under the tough guy’s skin,” another said.

But Obama was accused of “snobbery” by some Republican commentators. 

“Cheesecake Factory is a great option for people who can’t afford a private chef at their Martha’s Vineyard estate,” Matt Whitlock said in a post on X, referencing the Obamas’ estate on the exclusive island.

Trump’s Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, also made a statement by dining at the Cheesecake Factory in Washington, D.C. on Monday.

“I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try,” Bessent told Fox Business in a retaliatory dig at Obama.
news.summary: Obama previously said that Trump has ‘got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory’

news.title: Irish Examiner view: Government at odds with public mood in regards to data centres
news.text:
The protests come amid growing international opposition to the construction of ever-larger data centres. 

In the US, they have become a major issue in the midterm elections taking place this day week. Sixteen states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily halt new developments, while candidates from both Republican and Democratic parties have sided with communities resisting them. 

Opposition has now halted an estimated €64bn worth of new data centre projects.

Predictably, given the substantial financial support he has received from big tech, US president Donald Trump has dismissed opposition to data centres as “a sick conspiracy”.

The Government here has adopted a more measured approach, emphasising the economic importance of such centres to a country heavily dependent on the tech sector, while seeking to address concerns about energy consumption and carbon emissions.

However, the public remains unconvinced. 

An Irish Times/Ipsos B& poll last month found that more than 60% of respondents wanted the building of data centres to be halted, at least temporarily, with just 23% in favour of further construction.

While the immediate focus of next week’s protests will be the environmental consequences of data centres, their demands on the electricity grid, and their impact on local communities, it is likely that broader anxieties about the rapid advance of AI will also find expression. 

After all, the AI boom is driving the demand for more and bigger data centres.

The Government has a dilemma. It wants to keep Ireland positioned as an attractive destination for global technology, and ensure we are not left behind as AI develops. 

However, the infrastructure required to sustain that expansion comes at a cost, and the benefits cannot simply be assumed to outweigh the environmental, economic, and social consequences.

The challenge for the Government is to give a clear and credible explanation of why we need more data centres, who stands to benefit from them, and who will bear the costs. 

Unless it can make a convincing case that the national interest is being served by more data centres — and to date, it has not — it risks finding itself increasingly at odds with public opinion.

Small price for peace of mind

Last week’s disruption of digital bank Revolut’s services was a timely reminder of just how reliant we have become on digital payments and how quickly everyday life can be interrupted when they fail. 

Thousands of customers found themselves unable to access their accounts, pay for a morning coffee or transfer money.

As a nation, we have enthusiastically embraced cashless transactions, a trend accelerated by the covid pandemic, which made many people wary of handling notes and coins. 

A survey earlier this month found that 90% of purchases in pubs and nightclubs are now made with contactless payments, with just 5% made in cash. In retail, cash accounts for a mere 3% of transactions.

The convenience of cashless transactions is undeniable, but the Revolut disruption underlines the importance of having a backup. 

Irish holidaymakers learned the lesson the hard way last year when a major power outage in Spain and Portugal knocked out ATMs and electronic payments, leaving some unable to buy even a bottle of water.

Keeping a few euro in our pockets or wallet may seem old-fashioned, but it is a small price to pay for peace of mind.
news.summary: Some 60% of survey respondents in an Irish Times/Ipsos B&A poll stated they wanted the building of data centres to be halted
news.author: Irish Examiner,Irishexaminer.com
